entries.title: Mitch McConnell Is Denying Republicans His Massive Cash Stash
entries.summary: The outgoing senator has nearly $7.4 million to part with before leaving office in January. So far, he’s sitting on it.
entries.content:
Sen. Mitch McConnell is hoarding his committee’s wealth during a crucial midterms cycle for the Republican Party, according to a new federal filing.

When the Kentucky senator returned to Capitol Hill in September after a three-month, health-related absence, his campaign committee had nearly $7.4 million waiting for him.

But McConnell, who no longer has use for the money since he opted not to run for an eighth term, opted not to spread his wealth to any Republican Party committee or candidate campaign. That includes the Senate Leadership Fund and Texas PAC, political committees associated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who succeeded McConnell as the Republicans’ Senate leader.

Before McConnell leaves the Senate in January, his campaign committee has a few options for its surplus money.

Most urgently, McConnell’s committee can still donate up to $2,000 a piece to other Republican candidate committees. It may also transfer unlimited amounts to national party committees, such as the Republican National Committee or National Republican Senatorial Committee.

McConnell’s committee could also donate its millions to charities or nonprofit universities.

One organization McConnell is already connected to is the nonpartisan McConnell Center at the University of Louisville. The center was established in 1991 to encourage Kentucky’s top students to pursue higher education in their home state, and McConnell raised the initial funds for scholarships.

Other legal options include refunding donors or disgorging money to the U.S. Treasury’s general fund.

entries.title: Graham Platner’s Campaign Paid a $20,000 Severance to His Wife
entries.summary: The campaign also forked over payments to other staffers after the Democrat dropped out of the Senate race in Maine.
entries.content:
Graham Platner announced July 8 he was dropping out of the race for Senate in Maine.

Nine days later, his campaign paid his wife, Amy Gertner, $20,246 for “severance payroll.”

That’s part of the more than $350,000 Platner’s campaign paid out in severances, according to a filing with the Federal Election Commission. Others on the payroll received between $3,500 and $20,000 each in severance. Gertner received the most.

Gertner had a visible role on Platner’s campaign. When he came under scrutiny for sending sexually explicit texts to other women, Gertner filmed a selfie-style video defending her marriage and calling the stories “gossip.” Platner has denied the allegations, which later included a former girlfriend saying he had sexually assaulted her.

Campaign staffers, including Gertner, also received a $979 “win bonus” on July 3, a month after Platner’s primary victory.

Several staffers received severance payments of about $9,000. Some of them, per their personal LinkedIn pages, are current college students.

The campaign also paid out more than $70,000 in refunds to donors.

Platner’s team had more than $1.7 million on hand at the beginning of July. After campaign expenditures, severance and refunds, the campaign ended September with just about $99,000 remaining.

None of the leftover money went to Troy Jackson, Platner’s replacement in the race against incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins — perhaps due to political optics.

“That’s ‘Nazi accused rapist’ money,” a Democratic strategist told The Washington Sun in July. “The best thing he could do is give it to a women’s charity, specifically an organization supporting rape victims.”

Platner’s treasurer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sara Gideon, the Democrat who challenged Collins in 2020, still has $2 million in her campaign accounts. In recent months, she distributed $310,000 to Maine Democrats and $70,000 to other Democratic candidates across the country.

entries.title: Who’s Running Roger Marshall’s Campaign? His Campaign Filings Don't Say.
entries.summary: The Republican, who is in a heated race in Kansas, is facing questions about whether his Senate office is fueling his reelection campaign.
entries.content:
Sen. Roger Marshall’s latest campaign finance filing is largely missing spending entries typical of nearly all campaign reports: Those described as wages, salaries or payroll.

The Kansas Republican, who is up for reelection in a competitive race as Democrats try to expand their Senate map, is facing scrutiny about whether he’s used taxpayer dollars to fund his reelection bid, including by using his official Senate staff as an extension of his campaign.

Marshall’s latest filing with the Federal Election Commission, covering campaign spending from mid-July through the end of September, does not appear to include any payments to full-time campaign staff.

A joint investigation published last week by MS NOW and Kansas Reflector reported that the Marshall campaign hadn’t cut a paycheck to campaign staff in the last five years, an arrangement that experts quoted in the piece called “extremely uncommon” for a Senate campaign. The article also listed a number of instances in which Marshall may have violated ethics rules by using his office’s funds for campaign purposes.

Marshall’s office and the Marshall campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Marshall’s chief of staff told MS NOW and Kansas Reflector that the campaign now has campaign staff, without providing evidence.

Congressional staffers are allowed to work for campaigns, but only under strict guidelines. The work must be done on staffers’ own time, outside of congressional offices and without congressional resources.

The FEC filing says Marshall’s campaign spent $5.3 million in the third quarter, raising about $801,000 and finishing with $922,000 cash on hand.

The FEC records also indicate the campaign spent a little more than $10,000 on outside consultants from July through September.

Marshall, who polling has found to be deadlocked with Democrat Adam Hamilton, is in need of additional support for his campaign operation. According to Axios, Chris Grant, a top Trump political adviser who has previously worked for Marshall, is part of the cavalry that’s been sent in to help Marshall’s campaign in the final stretch.

The Washington Sun previously reported that Republican PACs have moved millions of dollars of ads into Kansas to rescue Marshall’s reelection bid as some GOP operatives say the senator lacks a good ground game.

entries.title: Labor's Trump-Appointed Watchdog Gets His Own Ethics Audit
entries.summary: Former Republican Rep. Anthony D’Esposito could face criminal charges if he is found to have violated objectivity standards.
entries.content:
Federal ethics investigators will audit the political conduct of Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D’Esposito, a former Long Island congressman accused of allowing partisan loyalties to affect his responsibilities as an impartial internal watchdog.

The U.S. Office of Special Counsel has “accepted the matter for review,” Newsday first reported Thursday, citing a letter sent this week to the nonprofit watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington. CREW filed the initial complaint against D’Esposito in April.

D’Esposito bristled when asked about the investigation, calling CREW a group of “political hacks” hawking “bogus nonsense.”

“It’s bullshit,” he told The Washington Sun Thursday evening. “I’ll keep exposing fraud and fighting for American workers.”

The ethics complaint against D’Esposito, who was appointed to the position last year by President Donald Trump, stems from a series of politically slanted social media posts the inspector general published using his official Labor Department X account.

He purportedly used the account to praise the president’s immigration and economic policies and congratulate him for his war efforts in Iran. In the April complaint, CREW chief executive Donald Sherman also pointed to numerous instances when D’Esposito accepted explicit direction from Trump and other administration officials.

“During his tenure as inspector general, D’Esposito has blurred the lines between official and political activities,” Sherman wrote.

The DOL inspector general is responsible for investigating fraud, waste and misconduct within the department and is legally required to remain objective and isolated from political pressures.

If the Office of Special Counsel finds that D’Esposito has flaunted objectivity standards, he could be fined, removed from office or face criminal prosecution for violating the Hatch Act's prohibitions against partisan activity.

Sherman also implored the Council of the Inspectors General on Integrity and Efficiency to act. D’Esposito said in a statement to Newsday that the council — another group that oversees integrity complaints against cross-agency inspectors general — is “taking no further action.”

Representatives from the council and the OSC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Musk Settles Lawsuits Over His $1 Million Election Giveaways
entries.summary: The Tesla founder promised voters checks before the 2024 presidential election, which critics said constituted election bribery.
entries.content:
Elon Musk and his political action committee have agreed to settle two lawsuits that accused them of misleading voters with promises of $1 million checks before the 2024 presidential election and in a 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election.

Legal counsel for the parties notified a federal judge in Texas that they’d struck an agreement to end the dual class-action suits Thursday. Terms of the settlements are not public and still require court approval.

The plaintiffs in the two cases — Arizona residents Jacqueline McAferty and Joy Harvick — accused Musk and America PAC of coaxing ⁠voters in seven swing states into signing his 2024 petition to support free speech and gun rights and submitting personal information for what they were told was a chance to receive $1 million. The giveaway was part of Musk’s broader effort to return Donald Trump to the White House.

The cases’ central claim, according to court filings, is that America PAC representatives vetted potential recipients of the prize rather than simply drawing names from a hat.

Following that blueprint, the tech mogul took the tactic to the March 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election to urge voters to turn out for Brad Schimel, the state's former Republican attorney general.

“I will also personally hand over two checks for a million dollars each in appreciation for you taking the time to vote,” Musk said in a now-deleted post on X.

Musk has already escaped a potential legal battle concerning his promises in Wisconsin: La Crosse County District Attorney Tim Gruenke declined to charge the tech mogul with election bribery in August, despite the state elections commission’s earlier ruling that he had likely broken the law. Gruenke, a Democrat, said no jury would have found Musk’s actions constituted election bribery.

America PAC, which is primarily funded by Musk himself, spent millions to support Schimel, who later lost to Susan Crawford.


The Tesla founder has denied the allegations of engaging in election bribery.

The Arizona settlements come weeks before November’s consequential elections. Musk, the wealthiest person in the world, has personally contributed over $275 million — more than any other person — to support the Republican Party’s efforts to retain its congressional majorities.

entries.title: Mary Peltola Dismisses Reports of Angry Outbursts as ‘Gossip’ During Debate
entries.summary: For the first time, the Democrat running in the high-stakes Alaska Senate race publicly addressed the reporting by The New York Times.
entries.content:
Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska’s Senate race, directly addressed allegations of mistreatment of former staffers for the first time on Thursday, calling them “outright fabrications” and “mass exaggerations of the truth” in a debate.

Peltola, who is running against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a close and widely watched race, has dodged questions on the campaign trail about the report by The New York Times from late September detailing mistreatment of staff. But at the hour-long Senate debate, the first time the candidates had faced off in such a setting, it came up several times.

Sullivan seemed eager to make it an issue, and brought up the allegations during an unrelated debate question.

“Take a look at how she treats Alaskans when the cameras are off. Look at that New York Times story,” he said, arguing it revealed a “character flaw.”

He alluded to some of the outlet’s reporting beyond Peltola’s behavior toward staff, including her alleged use of slurs.

The two began talking over each other, with Sullivan adding, “It’s The New York Times, read the article.”

Peltola jumped in to say the allegations were “gossip.”

The moderator threatened to shut off their microphones if necessary.

Later, a moderator asked Peltola directly about the allegations.

“I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day,” she said. “I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications or mass exaggerations of the truth.”

“I really am very concerned about making sure that we are respectful and respectful of all people, and again, this campaign is not about me on my worst day,” she added.

The Democratic candidate also suggested that the allegations likely emerged because her campaign is a threat to Sullivan. The incumbent senator once again circled back to the subject, pointing out that the report was not published by “conservative media” but rather the Times.

The Times reported that former staffers said Peltola had a history of frustration with staff throughout her campaign and as a member of the House of Representatives. It outlined an instance of her allegedly shoving a staffer, which her campaign characterized to the outlet as a bump. The report also included her alleged use of slurs, which Sullivan referenced as he attacked her over the article.

The story also described a text in which Peltola said of someone, “I hope she dies of a botched abortion.” That was also used as an attack line by Sullivan.

In a statement to the Times, her campaign spokesperson denied that she had a pattern of abusive behavior and cited a period of grief following the deaths of Peltola’s mother and husband in 2023.

The allegations shook the race in the closing stretch of the campaign, prompting an intraparty feud among Democrats about whether the staffers who shared their accounts with the Times had been too sensitive.

It was not a debate many Democrats liked taking up oxygen, given that the Alaska race has emerged as one of the most competitive in the country, with The Cook Political Report rating it a “toss-up.” Sullivan has served in his seat for two terms and Peltola was previously a U.S. House representative for Alaska’s at-large district.

It was clear how high the stakes were for both of them, as those were not the only heated exchanges.

Peltola appeared to read off notecards for much of the debate, which Sullivan noticed in real time.

"We weren't supposed to get these questions beforehand, were we?" he asked. (The moderators said no.) "I'm just watching my opponent read."

“I’m prepared,” Peltola responded.

entries.title: Donald Trump’s Legal Fund Is Flirting With Insolvency
entries.summary: Save America PAC is $1.9 million in debt after heavy summer spending.
entries.content:
Save America PAC — President Donald Trump’s preferred vehicle for paying legal bills — spent more than $5.1 million on legal bills during the third quarter, or around $56,000 per day, according to the committees’ latest filing to the Federal Election Commission.

That kind of spending has sent the leadership PAC — which is often pushing money out the door faster than it can come in — into legal debt topping $1.9 million.

Never Surrender, another Trump leadership PAC, helped to bail out Save America PAC by transferring from its account almost all of the $4.8 million Save America took in during the third quarter.

But it wasn’t enough to cover all of Save America’s legal bills, or the other $343,000 Save America spent on media consulting, payroll and other expenses, FEC records indicate.

Trump is a convicted felon who has faced numerous criminal and civil proceedings during the past several years, including a 2023 trial during which a New York jury found him liable for sexual abuse. Trump has also gone on the legal offensive of late, personally suing media organizations.

Neither Save America nor the White House immediately responded to requests for comment.

Save America has collectively paid more than two-dozen firms about $20.4 million for legal services and consulting since January 2025, when Trump began his second presidential term, according to FEC records. The PAC owes money to 12 of those firms, including two based in London.

Save America owes $761,000 to Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, the legal giant that has represented Trump in several high-profile legal battles, including the president’s unsuccessful appeal to the Supreme Court to overturn the $83 million defamation verdict that the writer E. Jean Carroll won.

The PAC also owes $663,000 to NechelesLaw LLP. Susan Necheles was one of the defense attorneys who cross-examined the adult-film actress Stormy Daniels during Trump’s “hush money” trial in 2024.

Brito PLLC, a Florida-based firm that has represented the president’s cases against news media giants including ABC News and The New York Times, is also owed $239,000.

Save America is also in debt $34,000 to the Dhillon Law Group, the firm founded by Harmeet Dhillon, who now serves in the Trump administration as assistant attorney general for the civil rights division at the Department of Justice.

The PAC also owes thousands of dollars to firms including New York-based criminal defense firm Tacopina, Seigel & DeOreo; Houston-based patent litigation firm Taylor Dykema PLLC; and civil rights and criminal defense firm James Otis Law Group LLC, among others.

entries.title: Kari Lake’s Old Senate Committee Is Still Stiffing Campaign Creditors
entries.summary: Lake awaits confirmation as U.S. ambassador to Jamaica. Her former campaign vendors together await more than $1 million.
entries.content:
Republican Kari Lake’s 2024 Senate campaign loss to Democrat Ruben Gallego is long behind her — except for the over $1 million in debt her campaign still owes two years later, according to a new Federal Election Commission filing.

Lake’s old campaign committee owes more than $328,000 to Opn Sesame for texting and telemarketing services and almost $278,000 to TAG LLC for “digital consulting & fundraising service.” The remaining over $400,000 in debts for online advertising and fundraising, however, are marked as “disputed.”

The seven-figure debt lingers as President Donald Trump’s nomination of Lake as U.S. ambassador to Jamaica has stalled — she has not yet received Senate confirmation despite the president nominating her in May.

The Lake committee isn’t without cash; it has nearly half a million on hand as of Sept. 30, according to its latest financial statement.

It’s also still processing a stream of contributions. Since July, Lake’s committee marked about $1,500 worth of this income as “debt retirement," meaning the money would directly go to paying off the campaign’s debt.

In the last year, the Lake campaign’s total debt fell by around $6,000, according to FEC filings, or about 0.6% of its current debt. Lake did not immediately respond to The Sun’s request for comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a Washington Sun inquiry.

Lake, an Arizona news broadcaster before her foray into politics marked by loyalty to Trump, has remained in the president’s close political orbit.

Last year, Trump appointed Lake as the “acting CEO” of the U.S. Agency for Global Media, which oversees Voice of America among other state-run foreign media outfits. In her first year, she oversaw massive downsizing.

In March, a federal judge ruled that both her chief role and cuts were illegal. Trump’s nomination of Lake for ambassador followed soon after.

entries.title: MS Forced Him to Retire From Politics. He Found a New Voice by Painting.
entries.summary: John Czwartacki spent decades as a political communicator, but he said painting felt like he “learned every language in the world.”
entries.content:
For decades, John Czwartacki made a career out of words.

He had worked and lived in D.C. since the ’90s, but in 2020, multiple sclerosis forced him into early retirement. The chronic disease, which affects the central nervous system, has been part of his life since his diagnosis in 1993. As it progressed, it affected his voice, making it increasingly difficult for him to communicate the way he once had.

“By 2020, I got to do so many things, so many great things. I traveled. I got jobs,” Czwartacki, better known as CZ, told The Washington Sun. “Unfortunately, I had the real reality of like, okay, well, I can't work in government. I can't work in a social office. Doctors are not really happy with me doing that.”

A longtime Republican communicator, Czwartacki served as press secretary for then-Rep. John Boehner and later as communications director for the Office of Management and Budget during President Donald Trump’s first term. His job was to shape messages, write speeches and explain the work of government.

For years following his retirement, Czwartacki struggled with what he described as a pent-up feeling, searching for a way to express an experience that spoken words could no longer fully capture.

Then, in November 2025, he bought a paintbrush and starter paints.

“Why is that? I'm not entirely sure,” he said. “I created pieces of art that I didn't expect to create, right? I didn't see that going in.”

As multiple sclerosis changed his relationship with his body and senses, painting opened up a new way to experience and interpret the world.

“I feel like a whole new set of senses was opened up to me. So it's like, wow!” he said. “A whole new suite of tactics to articulate myself are now available.”

For someone who had spent his career communicating through language, the discovery was revelatory.

“They're not things like words but you feel them and what is going on here is so cool as someone who has loved to communicate his whole life,” he said. “I'm like it's a whole new way to do it and I'm like, this is astounding to me.”
Mick Mulvaney, John Czwartacki (5171x3447, AR: 1.50)Czwartacki began experimenting with vibrant colors, fascinated by how they interacted on the canvas.

“Putting them close to each other and they would sing to each other and talk and leave you with a feeling of anticipation,” he said.

Less than a year after picking up a paintbrush, Czwartacki held his first art show on Oct. 8. The displayed paintings offered glimpses into the physical and emotional realities of living with a disease that has altered how he moves through the world — and how he sees himself.

The show was held in partnership with Survivors for Solutions, the nonprofit Czwartacki founded in 2022 to advocate for people facing health challenges who often struggle to make their voices heard in Washington.

Czwartacki painted “Hold On” while experiencing vertigo. Against a black background, white paint smears across the canvas, while a bright orange circle sits in the upper right corner.

The result is disorienting, an attempt to translate a physical sensation into something viewers can experience for themselves.

Another painting is an abstract self-portrait, a piece Czwartacki initially dreaded making.

He worried about his ability to draw recognizable features — “a nose or an ear or an eye” — but his son asked him to try.

The skeletal outline is fractured, he said, while the green near the bottom represents grounding. The background uses the same orange found in “Hold On,” a color that stands out against the more subdued elements of the portrait.

“I saw myself as incomplete and broken — still telling the story with things like this and also the MS,” he said. “And then the orange is kind of like shouting at you — it's paradoxical.”

The work does not attempt to neatly resolve the contradictions of his experience. Instead, the paintings hold them together: brokenness and expression, frustration and discovery, the limitations imposed by illness and the possibilities that remain.
John Czwartacki's paintings (5437x3624, AR: 1.50)Tina Robinson has known Czwartacki for over five years and founded an MS support group with him. She said he and his art are “proof that MS doesn’t get the final word.”

“As a patient myself, it’s inspiring to see him use the gift of time that new treatments have given us to find a new voice through his art,” Robinson said. “I hope his story inspires others living with chronic illness like MS or any challenging disease to take on new challenges and hold on to hope.”

Czwartacki may no longer be shaping political messages from inside the government, but he has not abandoned the impulse that drove him to the profession in the first place. He is still telling stories. He is still trying to make people feel something. He has simply found a different medium.

“I felt very proud of myself for my skill with English and my ability to write things and speeches and op-eds,” he said. “But when I learned to paint like this, I felt like I was taught every language in the world.”

entries.title: Trump’s Endorsement May Not Matter in the Next House Republican Leadership Race
entries.content:
There’s a big factor missing from the next race to lead House Republicans: President Donald Trump.

With House Republicans facing the prospect that they could be in the minority next year, and Trump himself entering the back end of his own lame-duck period, some believe the president’s influence won’t close the deal for Mike Johnson if he runs to remain the top elected leader.

“Not one bit,” one GOP lawmaker, given anonymity to speak freely, told The Washington Sun when asked if Trump’s endorsement matters. “Especially if we have lost, because people will blame him.”

Trump’s unique power has loomed over leadership races since Kevin McCarthy's bruising bid in 2023, when the president’s endorsement and personal phone calls helped sway some holdouts from blocking McCarthy’s path.

Trump intervened again during the next speaker’s race, after McCarthy was ousted 10 months later, when he thwarted Rep. Tom Emmer’s chances with a simple Truth Social post calling the Republican whip “totally out of touch.” And when Mike Johnson sought a full term as speaker in 2024, the president pressured some reluctant members to coalesce around Johnson to help him secure the gavel in 2025.

Heading into the next Congress, Republican lawmakers are split on Trump’s pull, with some saying it’s “not nearly as much” this round and others saying the president’s opinion would have some impact.

Johnson has made it clear he wants to lead his conference, whether or not Republicans maintain the majority. He currently has the backing of the president, who still thinks fondly of the Louisianan, according to two White House officials. But the path for Johnson won’t be easy, members say.

“He will not run unopposed,” one senior GOP member said.

Asked to comment on the speaker’s plan, a Johnson spokesperson referred The Sun to recent interviews with Johnson saying he believes Republicans will keep the majority and that he will remain the top leader.

But in an interview with Fox News recently, Johnson said he was unsure of what his next chapter would be if Democrats flip control of the House, saying that “if God moves on our hearts” he could go back to his hometown of Shreveport to start a “lawn business.”

Days later, in an interview with CBS News, he clarified his comments were "tongue in cheek” and added, “I would expect my colleagues would call upon me to continue to lead the conference in a divided government” if House Republicans lost the majority.

There are two other potential candidates laying the groundwork to lead the GOP conference next year. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise is popular with many members, who view him as personable, loyal and a savvy operator. And then there’s House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, who has been traveling and raising money for colleagues over the past year in what many view as building support to run for the top post.

Even if Johnson had Trump’s backing, that hasn’t always helped in the past. In 2023, following McCarthy’s ouster, Trump publicly backed Jordan for speaker over Scalise. However, on the private ballot, Scalise came out victorious.

Similarly, when Jordan did eventually get the nomination after Scalise dropped out, Trump’s endorsement didn’t translate into votes on the floor, as a bloc of members opposed him on multiple ballots.

Following the defeat, Jordan has been attempting to rebuild his image into someone who is a team player. He’s been in constant contact with the Republican conference through weekly, and at times daily, check-ins with his colleagues across the conference, multiple members told The Sun.

“Jim Jordan calls me every week, and he knows I wasn’t for him last time and not for him this time, and yet he still calls,” one lawmaker told The Sun.

Trump will have a bit more sway if Republicans retain the majority because lawmakers will have to publicly cast their ballot for speaker on the House floor. But, in the minority, members will vote via secret ballot the week after the midterms in a closed-door election, where Republican lawmakers say Trump’s power diminishes dramatically.

White House spokesperson Liz Huston, asked about Trump’s role, told The Sun, “President Trump is focused on maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

“If we win, then POTUS runs the show, as always,” one lawmaker, given anonymity to speak candidly, told The Sun. “But if we lose, he’s got a lot less stroke.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Representation Talks Taxation
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 16, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Possible tax hikes, Bard and the Guard and a red panda that needs a name. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. Warm for mid-October with some sunshine, but humidity, increasing winds and late-day storms take away a few points. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

D.C.’s license plates may say “Taxation Without Representation,” but today the city’s elected representatives will be discussing — you guessed it — taxation.

The D.C. Council is holding a long-awaited invite-only public hearing on possible tax hikes, covering everything from investment income and second homes to law firms’ and lobbyists’ currently untaxable proceeds, reports The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle.

The discussion comes at a time of profound change for D.C., with a new mayor set to take office in January but already facing a likely $600 million budget deficit and slowing economic growth.

“The city faces a big shortfall and we’re going to have to solve it either by cuts or revenue increases or a combination of the two,” said Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin.

Progressive groups and some lawmakers are pushing for tax increases on wealthy households, calling it a matter of simple fairness. One bill would impose a local version of an existing federal tax on proceeds from investment income for high-income households, while another would increase property taxes for second homes that aren’t occupied on a full-time basis.

“When you break it down to who’s paying what and you see that people who are making millions of dollars are paying lower tax rates than people who are struggling, it’s just not fair,” said Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, one of the main proponents of raising taxes.

Business groups and some tax skeptics counter that the worst time to raise taxes is when D.C. is already facing a slumping economy. “My worry is if we only do revenue and we only do weird goofy revenue things that no one else does, that’s going to hurt the long-term growth rebound,” said Joe Bishop-Henchman, the vice president of the National Taxpayers Union Foundation.

Today’s hearing is just the start of a conversation, and sources tell The Sun that it’s unlikely that anything will move forward before the end of the year. Still, what happens today could tee up big changes once Janeese Lewis George takes office, as she’s expected to on Jan. 2.





DEEP DIVE

“This is not a war zone”: Not long after classes let out at Bard High School in Congress Heights on Wednesday, a group of National Guard members stood nearby and watched as community members gathered to hold a meeting about their presence.

Parents and students, as well as community leaders like Ward 2 council member Brooke Pinto and Ward 8 State Board of Education member Dr. LaJoy Johnson-Law, held a listening session to discuss the impact of having armed troops marshalling a majority Black community, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.

“[Students] are watching armed personnel come outside their school, get ready for their duty, strapping guns [and] bulletproof vests on their body, dressing themselves in tactical gear,” said Kianna Faucette, vice president of Bard’s PTO.

A Bard senior reported seeing “[troops] outside my window in class.” Another student said he tries to “quickly walk past” the guard members. Bard parent Erica Brown said she has seen them out in the area as early as 6 a.m.

“I am a fourth generation Ward 8 resident,” Brown said. “Regardless of what people may say about us, this is not a war zone.”

Pinto said council members are considering a 1,000-foot buffer zone around schools, while Johnson-Law added that the state board of education is introducing a resolution that would allow high schoolers in the District to obtain REAL IDs so they can prove their age to guard members.





FROM THE DISTRICT

L'Enfant Plaza DC Metro (5814x3876, AR: 1.50)
Metro is using the L’Enfant Plaza station as a testing ground for new system-wide signage meant to make trains easier to find, board and exit. But, as The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports, some customers complain the signs are more disorienting than dependable.

Cockroaches in oatmeal, dead mice in salad, milk containers covered in mouse poop — those are just some of the disgusting dishes a new lawsuit alleges a D.C. jail has served people incarcerated there since July 2023, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

The Trump administration has formally invoked presidential communications privilege to withhold documents and block testimony about Donald Trump’s involvement in the Kennedy Center’s management, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports.

Lengthy elevator outages in D.C.’s public schools — some of which have persisted for months — are preventing students and teachers with disabilities or mobility issues from attending class and could violate their civil rights, The Washington Post reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Less than a month before Election Day, Alexandria residents found flyers citing federal laws that bar immigrants who are in the country illegally from voting, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. Alexandria Mayor Alyia Gaskins said in a statement to The Sun that she believes the flyers, which were stuck to cars in the area, are an attempt to intimidate voters. Though the flyers featured the U.S. Department of Homeland Security seal and phone number, a spokesperson said the department was not involved in their distribution.

Around 4,000 fewer students are enrolled in Fairfax County Public Schools compared to last year, following a trend of decreasing enrollment numbers felt across the DMV, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. This is the fourth consecutive school year FCPS has seen fewer students enrolled than the previous year.





FROM THE DINING ROOM


Tom Sietsema, The Sun’s food correspondent, writes about some under-the-radar cooking. 

A D.C. chef is serving a controversial fine-dining ingredient, albeit not by name. Diners have to ask their waiters for details about what’s cryptically listed among specials as “You Didn’t See This On the Menu.”

The dish? Foie gras, the fatty liver of duck (sometimes goose). The veteran chef offers two slices of the delicacy, marinated in whiskey, sugar and black pepper, with quince and apple, along with slices of brioche for $42.

On Nov. 3, District voters will decide whether to ban the sale of foie gras. Initiative 86, known as the Prohibiting the Force-Feeding of Birds Act, is backed by Pro-Animal D.C., an advocacy group that collected 45,000 signatures to qualify the measure. If approved, the ban would take effect in July 2027. Violating the law could result in fines as high as $5,000. The measure is opposed by the Restaurant Association Metropolitan Washington, among other groups.

The District chef I spoke to, whose name is omitted to avoid controversy, says he serves about half a dozen orders of foie gras on a busy night. “Why can’t I serve foie gras?” he asks. Referring to how other popular items are acquired, he adds, “What about cows and chickens?”





METRO MOMENT

Red Panda zoo (1179x1231, AR: 0.96)
The Smithsonian Zoo has welcomed a fiery new addition, and is asking for Washingtonians’ help in naming her. The female red panda cub — described as “bold” and “feisty” by the zoo — was born to parents Keahi and Rocket this past June.

Your three, pre-selected choices:

  • Dolly, after the legendary Dolly Parton.
  • Pyra, which the zoo says translates to “heat” in Greek, but historically has been used more morbidly to denote a funeral pyre.
  • Dolpa, after a Nepalese district home to wild red pandas.
You can cast your vote here.





SPORTS

What's it like to have kids in the NBA and WNBA at the same time? Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream tip off in the WNBA Finals on Saturday. Meanwhile, her brother, Julian, is preparing for the NBA season with the Pelicans. The Reeses are just one of the seven basketball families who are represented in both leagues. The Sun's Alex Schiffer caught up with a few of them to try and find the secret to raising a pair of pros.

entries.title: Morning Sun: What the Money Says
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Reading the FEC reports. Debate night in Alaska. The final Maine Senate match. The siren call of the “reach seats.” House Republicans prepare for a post-election leadership fight. And: Nebraska implemented Medicaid changes early, and Republicans are feeling the heat. 





THE LATEST

What’s in the FEC files: A particularly huge pile of money is sloshing around American politics right now, and this week is one of the few where we actually get to learn anything about it thanks to campaign finance laws. The Washington Sun’s Money & Influence Team (led by the inestimable, well-suited Dave Levinthal) pulled some of the big stories out of the FEC filings.

First, some smaller stories:

  • $978.68: The typical “win bonus” handed out by Democrat Graham Platner’s campaign after his Maine primary win.
  • $20,246.64: The “severance payroll” Platner’s camp gave his wife after the campaign ended.
  • $0: The amount paid to full-time campaign staff on Sen. Roger Marshall’s (R-Kansas) disclosures.
  • $2 million: The amount the campaign of Rep. Ralph Norman (R-South Carolina) is in debt to the congressman after a summer of losing two chances at a Senate seat.
  • $1.8 million: The amount Rep. Cory Mills (R-Florida) owes himself from his campaign after a worse summer than even Norman’s.
  • $260.60: How much the campaign of Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) spent at a nightclub in the Philippines. His summer was no prize, either. 
More: Musk Appears to Have Forked Over $158M to Help Paxton • Max Miller’s Campaign Is Deep in Debt — To Miller Himself • Will AOC Challenge Schumer in 2028? She Certainly Has a Cash Advantage. • Trump’s Legal Fund Is Flirting With Insolvency





FROM ALASKA


Debate notes: Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola directly read off note cards printed with tiny text so often at last night’s debate that Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan asked the moderators at one point if he was supposed to have gotten the questions in advance. Sullivan had notes, too, but appeared to ad-lib his answers a lot more.

Substantively, the debate featured Sullivan taking every opportunity to express disagreements with Donald Trump, particularly on the recent White House deal to import Russian diesel. Peltola defended herself against allegations she mistreated staff and attacked Sullivan over Trump policy moves like the war in Iran.

Changing color? “I believe it is turning purple. I can feel it,” former Democratic Sen. Mark Begich, a member of a long-running Alaska political family, told The Sun’s Alex Roarty on a recent trip to the state. “It’ll probably take two more cycles to prove it.”

Politics here is not like politics in the Lower 48. The State Legislature for years has had an unusual bipartisan, moderate power-sharing agreement to silence partisan extremists, Alex writes. Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski, another political scion, won a write-in reelection in 2010 after losing her primary to a Tea Party-backed candidate. Democrats think the GOP’s increasing shift away from a civil tone could open the door.

Republicans disagree, including Begich’s nephew Nick Begich, who is a Republican House member. “Alaska’s future is heavily dependent upon our ability to effectively advocate for resource development in our state,” he said. “And the Democrat Party, for whatever reason, has not been supportive of resource development in Alaska for many years.”

FROM MAINE


No love lost here: “Oh, shut up — I don’t even know that kid!” Democratic nominee Troy Jackson snapped at Republican Sen. Susan Collins during last night’s final debate of the Senate contest. That came after a member of the debate audience loudly interrupted Collins, saying, “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our waters,” and Collins labeled him one of Jackson’s supporters.

FROM ARKANSAS


Democrats’ French Hill conundrum: The Sun’s Paul Kane reports that Democrats are talking about spending resources to flip Arkansas’ 2nd District, which Hill has represented for years. It’s a sure sign the party is thinking about “reach seats,” places where, the theory goes, a little money could extend a blue wave. The problem, Paul notes, is that reach seats can be shiny objects that can distract from the actual battlegrounds where resources would be better spent. That’s what happened in 2020 — Democrats spent a lot on seats like Hill’s, only to see winnable races get starved for attention.

FROM A POTENTIAL FUTURE 


Shrinking-presidential-influence alert: “Not one bit” is how one GOP lawmaker described how much Trump’s wishes will matter in the next House Republican leadership race. “Especially if we have lost, because people will blame him.” The Sun’s Kadia Goba and Reese Gorman preview a chaotic Republican conference with the possibility of a sizable midterm loss — and with Trump’s power to select leaders diminished, Speaker Mike Johnson’s future is uncertain.

“He will not run unopposed” for another term as conference leader, a senior Republican lawmaker said. Already laying the groundwork to replace Johnson are Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN


Nebraska is running a Medicaid political experiment: The state imposed the Medicaid work requirements in the “one big, beautiful bill” in July, six months before it was legally required to do so. The impact has been swift: More than 1,000 people in the state have lost access to care so far. The Sun’s Avani Kalra reports that health care leaders, Republican observers and others now think it’s a key contributor to a political climate that suddenly has GOP leaders on the defensive in a state that’s reliably red.

“It’s gotten cast as you’re kicking people off health insurance and kicking people off government help,” said Perre Neilan, a Republican strategist in the state.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Launches ‘The Presidential Vibes Index’
entries.summary: The Washington Sun is launching a new editorial project about the 2028 presidential election.
entries.content:
The Washington Sun is launching a new editorial project about the 2028 presidential election that captures sentiment around which candidates are surging and which are floundering. Welcome to The Presidential Vibes Index.

Every month, a group of national reporters, pundits of all stripes, political scientists and other experts from around the country will rank a list of potential Democratic candidates and another of potential Republican candidates. That information will be combined with other attention markers like polling and prediction markets.

The result is a reported ranking that attempts to answer the question: Who is winning the primaries today?

The Sun’s Evan McMorris-Santoro is the lead writer of the project, working alongside The Sun’s data expert, Andrew Van Dam.

“There are always two conversations early in a presidential cycle: What do the polls say about a candidate and what is the vibe around that candidate?" McMorris-Santoro said. "With our panel of plugged-in experts, we're bringing these two things together. We'll tell you who is winning and who is losing and help readers understand the hard-to-define aura around a campaign.”

The panel will consist of roughly 60 participants. Contributors include: Kirk Bado, Leigh Ann Caldwell, Zoe Chace, Ruby Cramer, Daniella Diaz, David Drucker, Lee Drutman, Jesse Ferguson, Kadia Goba, Dana Milbank, Aaron Parnas, CJ Pearson, Alex Roarty, Elena Schneider, Alex Seitz-Wald, Marianna Sotomayor, Kara Swisher, Ben Terris, Jasmine Wright, Salena Zito and more to be announced in the coming weeks.

The Vibes Index will publish monthly, starting shortly after the midterms in November and continuing until the 2028 election.

About the Methodology

This is not a scientific poll — by design.

Participants’ first pick will get 10 points; their 10th pick will get 1 point. The secret sauce is the expertise of The Sun’s panelists, not statistics.

The Sun will publish the rankings for candidates of each party alongside polls, betting markets and other attention markers (such as Wikipedia traffic). Those figures will be measured against our experts’ vibes.

About The Washington Sun

We launched in 2024 as NOTUS, a news site focused on national politics and policy. But as we watched others pull back on Washington coverage, we knew our hometown deserved better. So we invested, more than doubling the size of our newsroom in just six months.

Our work puts Washington front and center, and we wanted our name to do the same. So NOTUS — short for News of the United States — is now The Washington Sun.

We cover politics and policy and the people who shape life in Washington — not just at the White House and in Congress, but at the Wilson Building, at Northwest Stadium and in the neighborhoods where we live.

We report for the people who live here, the people who make policy here and the people around the world who care deeply about what happens here. We do it with original reporting, with deep sourcing and with an unwavering commitment to accuracy.

Contact The Washington Sun

To participate in the experts panel, reach out to Evan McMorris-Santoro: ems@washsun.com. 

For press inquiries, reach out to Justin Peligri: JustinPeligri@washsun.com.

For sponsorship opportunities, reach out to partnerships@washsun.com.

entries.title: Alaska Is Becoming a Swing State
entries.summary: This year’s tight races are part of a decades-long trend. “I believe it is turning purple. I can feel it,” Mark Begich told The Sun.
entries.content:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — Mary Peltola is widely perceived — at least in Washington — to have a real chance at winning her marquee U.S. Senate race here because of her talent as a politician and a brutal national political climate for Republicans.

But there’s an overlooked factor boosting her campaign ahead of November’s election.

After being a firmly Republican state for most of its existence, Alaska has slowly but steadily moved left in recent elections, becoming more supportive of Democratic candidates at every level of elected office. By 2024, the state was more politically similar to right-of-center battlegrounds like Ohio and Iowa, where Democrats are often at least competitive statewide, than to the conservative strongholds like Wyoming and Idaho it used to resemble.

And unlike Ohio and Iowa, Alaska is continuing to move left: A Washington Sun analysis of presidential results found that from the 2000 election to 2024 election, Alaska shifted 20 points to the left relative to the national popular vote. That’s the fourth most of any state, trailing only Vermont, Colorado and Utah, according to the analysis.

From 2008 to 2024, it moved further toward Democrats than any other state, a 17-point shift. (The GOP performed especially well in Alaska in 2008 thanks in part to former Gov. Sarah Palin’s presence on the GOP ticket.)

The change is evident on the ground. In interviews with The Sun, more than a dozen party leaders, elected officials and political strategists described a state whose cities have become more progressive, whose state legislative battlegrounds have swung toward Democrats and whose top elected jobs — including one senator and governor — might soon be under the party’s control.

Democrats, cautiously optimistic about Peltola’s chances against Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, are even more bullish about the prospects of the party’s de facto gubernatorial nominee Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

It all leads to a conclusion that even some die-hard Democrats in Alaska are squeamish to admit after years and years of Republican dominance: Alaska might be becoming a genuine swing state.

“I believe it is turning purple. I can feel it,” said Mark Begich, a former Democratic senator. “It’ll probably take two more cycles to prove it.”

The state’s political evolution has big implications for its Senate race this year, which some party strategists are counting on to help Democrats gain the four seats they need for majority control of the chamber in 2027.

But, just as importantly, the transformation might offer a long-term lifeline for a Democratic Party with few viable targets in Senate races in the coming years, boxed in by a map filled with red states. And even though the state only carries three votes in the electoral college, its tiny sliver of votes could make the difference in tight presidential races when so many states are otherwise noncompetitive. The state’s White House result in 2024 was the 29th most friendly to Democrats, just behind Florida and Iowa, two states trending the wrong direction for the party.

Competing in Alaska might not be a question of something the party wants to do, but something the party has to do.

“If Democrats can’t consistently keep Alaska on the political battlefield, where else can they make that up?” said David de la Fuente, a political analyst with the Democratic think tank Third Way. “And it’s hard to make an argument for anywhere else.”
Dan Sullivan,Nick Begich,Julie Fate Sullivan (5115x3410, AR: 1.50)Initially, after being admitted as the 49th state in 1959, Alaska was seen as a state that would reliably vote for Democrats. But an oil boom in the 1960s on the state’s north slope transformed Alaska’s economy and its politics, bringing with it immense wealth and a wariness of the Democratic Party’s environmental agenda. Alaska last voted for a Democratic presidential nominee in 1964, when it backed Lyndon B. Johnson.

Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024, well short of the 25-point-plus victories George W. Bush racked up in the 2000s, but a double-digit victory nonetheless.

Alaska Republicans maintain that even if the margins are smaller than they used to be, the state remains reliably conservative at the federal level, in large part because of the incompatibility of the national Democratic Party’s environmental policies and the state’s economic needs.

“Alaska's future is heavily dependent upon our ability to effectively advocate for resource development in our state,” Republican Rep. Nick Begich said in an interview. “And the Democrat Party, for whatever reason, has not been supportive of resource development in Alaska for many years. And they've proven that as a core component of their national platform, they are not willing to support resource development in our state.”

Nick Begich, who also faces a competitive race this year against the Democratic-backed independent candidate Bill Hill, pointed out that Democrats like former senator Mark Begich and Peltola had won statewide general elections in Alaska before (in 2008 and 2022, respectively) only to lose their next election. It’s a sign, he said, that even if voters here are willing to give Democrats a chance, they’re rarely willing to stick with them after they’ve been in office.
Election 2026-Alaska (5184x3456, AR: 1.50)Even the most bullish Democrats say that even if the state is trending their way, it will always retain a distinct political independence. Alaska’s unique characteristics — its oil and fishing industries, native Alaskan population and rugged arctic climate — mean its politics are unlike any other state’s, often less ideologically driven and more focused on demanding basic material support for communities that would suffer without it.

It’s why the state elected an independent governor last decade and why the state legislature for years has had an unusual power-sharing agreement between Democrats and moderate Republicans, designed to exclude extreme voices in either party. It also explains how Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski won a write-in reelection campaign in 2010 after losing her primary to a tea party-backed candidate, drawing support from across the political spectrum.

Still, some Democrats have quietly touted Alaska’s emerging importance for years, especially after Peltola’s 2022 victory in the state’s at-large House seat. De la Fuente, the Third Way official, wrote an analysis in 2023 urging then-President Joe Biden to consider competing in the state during the next presidential election.

The state’s demographic profile — including a low share of white voters, relatively high union participation and low religiosity — aligned with the modern Democratic Party, he wrote at the time, and was a major reason the state had shifted to the left over the previous two decades. In his view, Alaska represented a much better bet for Democrats than states like Florida, Ohio and Iowa, which received considerably more attention as potential battlegrounds.

“I feel like the political data is telling a very strong story here, of this not being a fluke,” de la Fuente told The Sun.
APTOPIX Vance (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Why Alaska has shifted politically is a subject of debate. The state’s electorate, on the surface, has not changed significantly since 2000, according to Census data.

Some political strategists point to the declining number of oil and gas jobs, which started last decade and intensified after the 2020 pandemic and proliferation of remote work. Others say Alaska’s unusual open primary system, implemented in 2022 in which the top four vote getting candidates move on to the general election, has contributed, helping Democrats nominate more moderate candidates they consider better aligned with the state.

But locally, Democrats point to two main factors: the evolution of politics in Anchorage and the priority local Democrats place on political pragmatism.

Anchorage, at a population of nearly 300,000 people, holds about 40% of the state’s total population. And at a local level, its politics have shifted left.

Mark Begich recounted that as a young Democrat running for a seat on the city assembly here in the 1980s, every level of elected office in the town’s eastern half — from governor down to local legislator — was represented by a conservative or Republican (the city’s assembly seats are nonpartisan). Now, east Anchorage is represented at every level of state government by liberals or Democrats.

Across the city, local politicos say a 12-member assembly that used to be evenly split ideologically is now almost uniformly liberal, save for one or two members.

“Anchorage growing up is part of the story,” said Eric Croft, chair of the state Democratic Party. “Anchorage is getting to be a medium-sized city that, like a lot of them, is getting more and more progressive.”

Anchorage, in other words, is following the same political path of a lot of cities across the country.

“People that are living in Anchorage want good schools for their kids and actually want parks and amenities,” said Jim Lottsfeldt, an independent political strategist. “And there's sort of been a maturation process of what we expect from our government and what we want as far as public facilities.”

To other Democrats, it’s hard to miss how the state’s leftward drift over the past 20 years corresponded with the rise of the tea party movement and, later, Trump — two ideologically driven movements they argue are at odds with the state’s pragmatic bent.

“I think Alaskans, given their druthers, would vote for a nice Chamber of Commerce Republican,” said Joelle Hall, emeritus president of the Alaska AFL-CIO. “A banker. A nice guy. A civically minded, slightly conservative guy. That's their drug of choice.”  

“That's not what's been offered to them lately,” Hall said.

In 2000, with George W. Bush on the ballot, Alaska voted 31.5 percentage points to the right of the country (Bush won Alaska by 31 points while losing the national popular vote by one-half of a point). In 2024, with Trump again leading the GOP ticket, the state voted just 11.5 percentage points to the right of the nation (Trump won Alaska by 13 points while winning the national popular vote by 1.5 points).

Democrats are emphatic that the quality of the individual candidate on the ballot is hugely important in Alaska. It’s why they don’t think that Murkowski, who has done more to separate herself from Trump than perhaps any other Senate Republican, will face a serious challenge from Democrats when she’s up for reelection in 2028.
Capitol Hill (4680x3120, AR: 1.50)It’s also why in-state Democrats are most skeptical about the party’s presidential chances in Alaska anytime soon. The party’s White House nominee usually has a different, more ideological profile than the types of candidates Democrats run in the state. Peltola’s views on energy development, for instance, would likely draw a fierce backlash from national Democrats’ progressive base.

Even progressives in the state say that Democrats run a different kind of campaign in Alaska than elsewhere.

“Those of us who are progressive have embraced bipartisanship,” said Zack Fields, a Democratic state representative who represents part of Anchorage. “And rather than talk about whatever crazy identity politics that has seized the national Democratic Party, we talk about bread-and-butter issues that affect families every single day. We talk about class size, we talk about energy security, we are just relentlessly pro-jobs.”

Fields said that if Democrats nationally embraced the approach he and his colleagues have taken in Alaska, they “would have 85% of the seats in Congress.”

But, he added, the state is often overlooked by the national party. It’s why its shift to the left this century has been largely ignored, even if it could help the party win a Senate majority this November.

“People in the Lower 48 are not aware of it,” Fields said. “If Alaska were the geographic distance to D.C. of West Virginia or another state nearby, there’d be all kinds of stories about it because it’s super interesting.”

entries.title: Filipino Nightclub, Parisian Restaurant: Rep. Dan Crenshaw’s Campaign Went Traveling
entries.summary: Federal records indicate the Texas Republican, who lost reelection, made a series of uncommon international expenditures.
entries.content:
The campaign committee of Rep. Dan Crenshaw went globe-trotting, dropping thousands of dollars on foreign travel expenses from France and Italy to Croatia and the Philippines, according to Crenshaw’s most recent filing with the Federal Election Commission.

Crenshaw lost in a Texas Republican primary in March and will exit Congress in January.

The campaign reported spending around $1,200 on “event catering” at a Croatian Michelin star restaurant, $490 for “meeting expense[s]” between a Filipino nightclub and Parisian restaurant and nearly $320 for lodging at a boutique hotel in Rome, FEC records indicate.

From late July through September, the campaign reported spending over $9,000 on airfare. The bulk of that money funded flights with United Airlines, but the campaign additionally used two Greek airlines and Air France over the last three months.

While not international, Crenshaw’s campaign also dropped nearly $700 on “event catering” at Casa Tua’s Aspen, Colorado, restaurant and lounge in August, according to FEC records.

The purpose and exact timing of these trips is unclear. The Crenshaw campaign reported paying for them during July, August and September. A representative for Crenshaw could not be reached for comment Thursday evening.

Running in a redrawn district, Crenshaw lost to Steve Toth, a conservative member of the Texas House of Representatives, who slammed the congressman for rejecting claims of fraud in the 2020 election.

While Crenshaw couldn’t get President Donald Trump’s endorsement, Toth was backed by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, Turning Point Action and the Freedom Caucus Fund.

“A large part of this election was about the power of clickbait … Memes became truth. Too many people are not discerning through the clickbait,” Crenshaw told The Texas Tribune after his loss. “The truth didn’t matter to people.”

entries.title: The ‘Reach’ Seat Conundrum Facing Democrats
entries.summary: History rarely offers chances to flip some seats, but temptation sometimes distracts from core races.
entries.content:
Here we go again.

It’s late in the campaign season and the party out of power feels a big jolt of momentum and starts hyping races that insiders call “reach seats,” the House or Senate races that seem safely in the hands of one party but once a generation seem to open up for the other side.

Last week House Democrats highlighted the opponent of Rep. French Hill (R-Arkansas) as “worthy of additional investment” because the political environment has broken so much against Republicans that the six-term incumbent could be defeated.

Hill, who chairs the House Financial Services Committee, was one of a dozen Republicans targeted anew by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, despite his always large stockpile of campaign cash and representing a district that favored Donald Trump by double digits all three times he’s run for president.

Over the last 20 years each party can point to times that investing in “reach” seats paid off. For Democrats the 2006 and 2008 elections gave them historically large majorities that stretched from places like Boise, Idaho, through all of North Dakota and even a majority of Alabama’s House delegation. That paved the way for the passage of the Affordable Care Act and a Wall Street reform bill in 2010.

Big Republican wins in 2010 and 2014 gave them their biggest House majority since the 1920s, opening the doors to the 2017 tax cuts and a durable Senate majority that confirmed three conservative Supreme Court justices.

But recent history is filled with examples of the temptation to go bigger leading to the political equivalent of Lucy pulling the football away from Charlie Brown.

That’s what happened the last time Democrats chased after Hill, back in 2020, when their outside groups poured more than $3.5 million into a failed effort at that seat.

Hill won easily, by almost 11 percentage points, and nationwide Democratic hopes for gaining 10 to 15 seats or more crashed into an unexpected undertow. Republicans gained more than 10 seats on Election Day despite Trump losing the popular election by 7 million votes, a historic anomaly that happened only once before in the previous 14 elections.

“I do think they took their eye off the ball in some places,” Parker Poling, who was the executive director of the National Republican Congressional Committee in 2020, told The Washington Sun.

Even when Hillary Clinton and Al Gore lost the Electoral College in 2016 and 2000, respectively, their popular vote margins of more than 500,000 and almost 3 million helped House Democrats win a few seats down the ballot.

Instead of a historically large majority in 2021, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi had just 222 seats, and every vote became a bit of a cliffhanger.

Two years later Republicans fell victim to their own overly ambitious ways ahead of the 2022 midterms, pouring tens of millions of dollars into districts where wins turned out to be mirages.

Their lone reach seat victory came against Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-New York), who was chairing the DCCC that cycle. Pelosi told Democrats the day after the election that Republicans spent so heavily to go after Maloney that it helped preserve other Democrats.

“Our chairman took an arrow for us,” she said.
Election 2020 Arkansas House (1572x1048, AR: 1.50)When the dust settled, Republicans gained just nine seats, leaving them at the same exact skinny majority the Democrats had — 222 seats. It set the stage for a dysfunctional House for the next four years.

Senate campaigns also often take fliers on seats that seem well out of reach in normal times, but the payoff can be much higher given the reward is a six-year term that can help sustain a majority not just in the coming election but over the next two.

Without upset wins in Louisiana in 2002 and Montana in 2006, Senate Democrats wouldn’t have had sufficient votes to pass the ACA in 2009 — which has some party operatives dreaming of pulling off upsets in November in such traditionally conservative states like Kansas or Alaska.

Now, House Democrats are feeling confident about their standing in the traditional battleground seats: Of the 21 “toss-up” races, 15 are held by Republicans, according to one independent analysis, while seven more of their seats already “lean Democratic.”

“Democrats must build a durable majority heading into the 120th Congress so that the House can deliver wins,” Julie Merz, executive director of the DCCC, wrote in a fundraising memo last week.

She is trying to raise cash fast for a handful or more of these reach seats. By siloing them into their own financial category, Democrats are hoping to avoid losing focus on their core races the way they did in 2020.

Republicans rejected these Democratic moves as either attempts to trick them into spending money in places that they don’t need to, or just the equivalent of online trolling. The math in these seats, they say, simply doesn’t add up to Democratic wins.

“These seats are staying red, and Republicans are on offense across the map,” Mike Marinella, national press secretary for the NRCC, said.

In a reminder of the 2022 campaign, Democrats listed the seat of Rep. Richard Hudson (R-North Carolina), chair of the NRCC since early 2023, as a possible target.

Hudson won his district by almost 19 percentage points in 2024, as Trump won it by 16 points, about the same as his margin of victory in 2020.

Moreover, Merz’s memo also listed the seat of Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-New York) as a potential pickup opportunity, now that the onetime rising conservative star is retiring.

The temptation is there to try to win such a symbolic victory for Democrats after Stefanik’s midcareer transformation into a fire-breathing, MAGA-loving Trump acolyte.

Yet Democrats would be trying to win a seat that Stefanik, first elected in 2014 as a moderate, establishment-friendly Republican, won by almost 25 percentage points in 2024, when Trump carried the district by more than 20 points.

Trying for those seats almost sounds more exotic than Republicans in 2022 reaching for the Orange County, California, seat held by Katie Porter, whose progressivism irked many conservatives. Republican-aligned outside groups shoveled more than $10 million into trying to defeat her.

That’s more than double the $5 million those same Republican groups poured into trying to win a Rhode Island district that Democrats have held since 1991. Joe Biden had just won those seats by 10 points or more, just as he had done in Maloney’s seat.

Those races were close, but Democrats won. Meanwhile, Republicans lost several close races in the Midwest that were on much more friendly terrain, including three in Ohio that broke against them even as Republican Gov. Mike DeWine won reelection at the top of the ticket in a landslide.

Poling, who ran the NRCC in 2020, said she heard Democrats thought they could win a handful or more Republican seats in Texas alone.

“I just don’t see it,” she told The Sun, recalling the message she sent her staff to run their numbers again.

Democrats did not win a single close seat in Texas that year. They lost all 27 seats that The Cook Political Report rated as toss-ups in its final race ratings.

In fact, Republicans came within less than 32,000 votes of winning five other races, which would have won them the majority, a virtually unheard of concept given their candidate lost the presidential election.

Republicans got their trophy seat in 2022 by defeating Maloney, the first time a campaign committee chair had lost reelection in 30 years. His district, partially in the New York City media market, received an endless amount of ads, backed by more than $10 million from outside conservative groups trying to boost now-Rep. Mike Lawler’s upstart campaign.

In the end, Lawler won by less than 1 percentage point, less than 2,000 votes, and Maloney had the odd pleasure of being hailed for his stewardship of the DCCC and mitigating their losses but losing his own seat.

The next day he said the key to their national strategy was sticking to the plan.

“We resisted the temptation to chase shiny objects, and we were disciplined and focused, and we did the work. And I'm a big believer in doing the fundamentals,” Maloney told reporters.
