entries.title: The Habits of Highly Effective Basketball Families
entries.summary: There are seven families who have both a daughter in the WNBA and a son in the NBA this year. They shared some of the secrets to their success.
entries.content:
Angel Webb Reese was fed up.

It was the mid-2010s, and for the past few years, her daughter, Angel, and son, Julian, would go outside their home in Randallstown, Maryland, to play one-on-one basketball in their single-car driveway.

But getting through a game became difficult.

Tempers flared between the siblings, and the games got physical. Even when kids from the neighborhood joined in and they started playing five-on-five, the games would turn into one-on-one sibling battles, with the other players turning into spectators, watching the Reeses go at it.

“We would fight a lot,” Julian says now. “Especially when people were around.”

Webb Reese ultimately took the hoop and put it in the neighborhood dumpster after years of bickering between her kids.

“I did not realize how competitive it would become with the both of them,” she said. “They would nearly kill each other out there.”

The lessons from those one-on-one matchups have been on display for the Reeses throughout the year. Julian made his NBA debut with the Wizards this past year and opens the season with the New Orleans Pelicans. Angel is a star on the Atlanta Dream, which is currently in the WNBA Finals.

The family is one of seven who have a son and a daughter playing in the NBA and WNBA, along with the Williams, Ruperts, Salaüns, Prospers, Jaquezes and Coffeys.

More professional sibling duos could be on the way. Mystics center Lauren Betts has a younger brother, Dylan, who is a top 10 recruit nationally. Atlanta Hawks rookie Kingston Flemings, a Virginia native, has a younger sister, Bella, who was one of the nation’s top recruits a year ago and is now a freshman at Duke. (Pacers guard T.J. McConnell’s sister, Megan, spent the preseason with the Indiana Fever but didn’t make their opening-night roster.)

The NBA does not officially keep track of families who have competed in both leagues. (If the league is looking for a way to feature them, Sixers wing Rayan Rupert, whose sister Iliana plays for the Golden State Valkyries, suggested that the NBA create an event at All-Star weekend where each active sibling duo competes to see who’s No. 1.)

But there have been a few significant sets over the years. Houston Rockets coach Ime Udoka and his sister, Mfon, were the first siblings to play in both leagues in 2003. Hall of Famer Candace Parker and her older brother, Anthony, now the Orlando Magic GM, are another notable pair. (Perhaps the most famous basketball sibling duo doesn’t qualify for this distinction, as Cheryl Miller was a star before the creation of the WNBA, while little brother Reggie went on to a legendary NBA career.)

What are the secrets to these families’ success? Genes are certainly a factor. Six of the seven families with kids in both leagues have at least one parent who played in college or beyond. But there are also many basketball values that these families share — and those lessons rival the bloodlines that produced professionals in both leagues.

Lesson No. 1: Hustle Matters More Than Skill

Before she became one of the DMV’s most famous basketball mothers, Webb Reese was a star at Maryland-Baltimore County, where she played beyond her frame.

A 5-foot-11 forward, she averaged 13.2 rebounds per game in her senior year at UMBC. She passed that rebounding trait on to her kids. Angel Reese led the WNBA with 12.1 rebounds per game in the regular season and recently became the fastest player in league history to grab 1,000 boards. Julian averaged nine or more rebounds in his last two seasons at Maryland and averaged 10.5 rebounds in 13 games with the Wizards this past season.

But Webb Reese never gave her children any formal lessons in rebounding. Or shooting. Instead, she harped on hustling. Julian can still hear her voice shouting at him whenever he wasn’t sprinting down the court.

“She told us if we run the floor, play as hard as we can, everything is going to come to us,” Julian said.

“I was aggressive, tenacious. I had a high motor, which I think both of my kids both have,” Webb Reese said. “I always just said ‘box out,’ because I think a lot of times rebounding has to do with your effort.”

Olivier-Maxence and Cassandre Prosper’s parents took a similar approach. Gaetan and Guylaine Prosper met playing college basketball at Concordia University in Montreal, then proceeded to coach their kids when they became parents. According to Guylaine, they stressed knowing “the why of things”: emphasizing their rationale for how something like sprinting versus jogging for a loose ball could make a difference.
Dream Mystics Basketball (2895x1930, AR: 1.50)Olivier-Maxence Prosper, now a forward with the Memphis Grizzlies, struggled to recall a game in which his parents were upset with him because of a bad shooting night or foul trouble.

“They really only got us for mistakes on effort,” Prosper said. “If we didn’t put in effort, that’s when they got mad.”

The Prosper children have become the first Canadian siblings to play in both leagues, and they still get texts full of feedback from their parents after every game. Olivier-Maxence said most of his mother’s comments will be about plays where he failed to crash the boards or didn’t hustle hard enough.

“To this day, they’re always coaching effort,” Cassandre Prosper, who now plays for the Mystics, said.

Lesson No. 2: Versatility Over Specialization

Before he was the father of two professional basketball players, Larry Parker was a small forward at Iowa in the 1970s trying to get more playing time. Parker had a good feel for the game and could pass but wasn’t an elite shooter or playmaker, which hindered his ability to regularly get on the court. His oldest son, Anthony, said his father used his reputation as a defensive stopper as a ticket to more playing time.

Larry went on to have three kids, and when they took up the game, he wanted their careers to look different from his.

“He was determined to make us versatile enough to where no matter what situation we ran into, we wouldn’t just fall back into one thing,” Anthony Parker said.

Larry trained all three kids the same way — prioritizing fundamentals and teaching them a little bit of everything, from shooting to post ups to ballhandling. The goal was to ensure they didn’t have a weakness, giving their coaches little reason to take them out. Anthony grew to be 6-foot-6, his dad’s height, and played nine years in the NBA before becoming a front office executive.

His sister, Candace, had a much different career. Considered one of the greatest women’s basketball players of all time, she won three WNBA championships with three different teams and two NCAA titles at Tennessee, excelling with a skill set rarely seen in a player of her size.

“She's 6-foot-4 and basically the height of a center in the women’s game,” Anthony said. “But you add in the fact that she can do all of the things guards and wings can do, and that’s what set her apart.”
BASKETBALL: AUG 15 Basketball Hall of Fame Enshrinement Ceremony (3900x2610, AR: 1.49)One summer, Candace Parker recalled her dad coming up to her with a simple message: “You should get better with your left hand.”

So Candace spent her summer doing a little bit of everything with her left hand.

“I can remember eating with my left hand one summer,” Candace said. “I remember brushing my teeth with my left hand, doing [left-handed] push-ups during commercials.”

Gaetan Prosper posed a question to his kids that was similar to Larry Parker’s.

“How can you always be an asset on the court?” he would ask them.

The Prospers had their kids play every position on the court when they were growing up, even if it wasn’t a natural fit. At minimum, they would understand the roles and responsibilities each position required and know how to play off it.

At Notre Dame, Cassandre Prosper was one of the most multidimensional players Niele Ivey ever coached. In her senior year, she averaged 13.6 points, 6.5 rebounds, 1.6 assists, 1.6 steals and 1.1 blocks per game, stuffing the stat sheet while leading the Irish to their first Elite Eight in years. Ivey said Prosper operated like a professional and understood the game at a level few college players can relate to.

“Having parents who played at the highest level, they understood what it takes to be a separator,” Ivey said.

In 1997, Angela Jaquez tried out for the upstart Los Angeles Sparks ahead of the WNBA’s maiden season. Her professional dreams ended there, but this past spring, she became the latest parent to have a kid in each league after her daughter, Gabriela, was drafted by the Chicago Sky. She joined Jamie Jr., who plays for the Bucks after starting his career with the Heat.

Both Angela and her husband, Jamie Sr., were standouts at Concordia University Irvine and coached Jamie Jr. and Gabriela as kids.

“You need to be able to pass and dribble, to be able to run a play, so that was what we focused on,” Angela Jacquez said.

She said they started having their kids watch film as early as elementary school to teach them about the flow of the game and show them ways they could move without the ball to help their teams win. They didn’t begin teaching the kids proper shooting form until they thought they were strong enough — a practice that NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson’s father, Rick, a former NBA player himself, also applied.

“Doing the little things is going to lead to big results,” Angela Jaquez said. “Everybody wants flashy plays. Those can happen, but you have to do the basics.”

Lesson No. 3: Competition Helps Everyone

When Elizabeth Williams was at Duke, she made history as the first player ever to win ACC Defensive Player of the Year four consecutive years.

But when she came home to Virginia Beach, her defensive genius within her family was waning. Elizabeth is eight years older than Mark, which put him in middle school during his older sister’s historic run. Around that time, he outgrew her 6-foot-3 frame en route to his current height of 7 feet. (He now plays center for the Phoenix Suns.) Their one-on-one games ended shortly after.

“She would play me when I wasn’t the player I am,” Mark said in a joint interview with his sister last year. “She knew she was gonna win.”

“He was probably 6-8 [when he won],” Elizabeth replied. “Let’s be real.”




That competitive dynamic prevailed across every set of siblings interviewed for this story. While parents emphasized different aspects of the game, their kids applied the teachings against each other until one sibling outgrew the other.

“It was even in the beginning,” Julian Reese, who is 6-foot-10, said. “But towards the end I was just winning.”

Lauren Betts is one of the tallest players in the WNBA at 6-foot-7. She dominated games against her brother when he was little.

“Dylan, when he was small, the girls would kind of beat him up,” Michelle Betts, Lauren’s mother, said. “And it was really upsetting for him. But as he got bigger, I feel like it was three or four years ago where they were like, ‘We can’t beat Dylan anymore.’”

The shift in competitiveness against her brother has given Betts a new perspective. Given her height, she was always used to being the tallest one on the court.

“I feel like going against my brother is crazy to see how other people feel going against me,” Betts said. “It’s kind of like karma.”
WNBA: SEP 27 Playoffs Washington Mystics at Atlanta Dream (5700x3800, AR: 1.50)But the matchups have borne fruit as the siblings' careers have advanced. Unlike Betts, Angel Reese regularly goes up against players taller than her, and her mother sees her using the same moves against opponents that she tried on Julian years earlier. That was on display in September at the FIBA World Cup when Reese was matched up against China center Zhang Ziyu, who, at 7-foot-3, is a footer taller than her.

“Going against her brother and his strength allowed her to use that to her advantage now,” Webb Reese said. “When she’s in the league now going against women who are stronger and taller than her, she uses what she learned when she was playing against her brother.”

Reese, who briefly played on the same team as her brother and his friends growing up, said that playing with him ultimately benefited her — even if it wasn’t the most enjoyable experience.

“He definitely helped me get tougher,” Angel Reese said. “I was the only girl on the team, and he worked me up a lot and told me I wasn’t good. He was definitely my biggest critic but also helped me a lot.”

That help continues for many of the siblings to this day. While their parents may have provided the lessons that helped get them to the pros, the siblings now have the perfect confidante to help manage the challenges of playing pro basketball.

That is particularly true for the Williamses, who are the only NBA-WNBA family without a parent who played at a high level. Alex works as a gastroenterologist and Margaret was a nurse. When Elizabeth expressed interest in basketball as a kid, they bought her “Basketball For Dummies,” given their lack of experience with the game.

As both kids have become professionals, the parents have seen them go to each other for help, which is exactly the way they want it.

“If Mark has anything basketball related, he will talk to Elizabeth before he talks to us,” Alex Williams said. “Which is good, because we can't be that.”

entries.title: With Budget Gap Looming, D.C. Council Starts Talking About Tax Increases
entries.summary: The revenue is tempting, but critics say the last thing the city’s weak economy needs right now is tax hikes.
entries.content:
In what could be viewed as either a necessary attempt to correct D.C.’s historic economic inequalities or a foolhardy push to soak the rich amidst a downturn in the city, on Friday the D.C. Council will start debating a range of possible tax increases that could hit everything from investment income and second homes to law firms’ and lobbyists’ currently untaxed proceeds.

The hearing represents the first time in years that lawmakers have dived into the details of whether — and how — to raise more revenue and make the tax code fairer. It also comes at a time of profound change for D.C., with a new mayor set to take office in January but already facing a likely $600 million budget deficit and slowing economic growth.

“The city faces a big shortfall and we’re going to have to solve it either by cuts or revenue increases or a combination of the two,” said Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin. “The track record of the city has been to come forward with a revenue raiser at the last minute in the budget process with no deliberation around it. What this hearing is is a constructive conversation about what are our options.”

While there are differences of opinion on the wisdom of raising taxes — and how D.C. could do it — this much is uncontested: The city’s economy and the growing revenue streams it long provided lawmakers are down, in part because of a return to normality that never happened after the pandemic and also the more recent cuts to the federal workforce that have cost the city more than 36,000 jobs in the last year.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The council has already had to deal with two difficult budget cycles that saw increasing fights over smaller pots of money for social services that have gotten more expensive — even as the need for them has remained steady.

“For the past several years we’ve said, ‘Maybe we need to wait until everyone is back in the office and DOGE is done and tourists are back.’ So we’ve been doing a lot of one-time things, and we’re coming to the end of these measures,” said Joe Bishop-Henchman, vice president of the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, an Advisory Neighborhood Commission member in Ward 5 and one of the 23 invited witnesses who will be testifying at Friday’s hearing.

“That only leaves hard decisions on spending and revenue,” he adds.

That’s especially the case now, as D.C. faces an estimated 2028 budget deficit of $600 million to $800 million that the new mayor — expected to be Ward 4 council member Janeese Lewis George — will be saddled with.

A number of tax-increase ideas have already been floated by lawmakers and hinted at by Lewis George, and those will serve as a foundation of today’s discussion. One, proposed by Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau, would take an existing federal tax on investment income and apply it locally to wealthy residents. The tax would produce an estimated $200 million in revenue the first year and $100 million a year after.

“The discussion around the Wealth Proceeds Tax comes down to the fact that we tax 100% of other types of income, so why aren’t we taxing these other sources of income? It’s just a matter of fairness,” Nadeau told The Sun. “People at the very top are doing very well, and it’s not an onerous tax.”

This isn’t the first time Nadeau has proposed raising taxes on wealthy households. In 2021 she led a successful charge — joined by Lewis George — to increase marginal tax rates on residents who make over $250,000 a year, with the revenue directed to cover pay increases for child care workers, more housing vouchers for homeless residents and expanded tax credits for low-income families.

But for Yesim Sayin, executive director of the D.C. Policy Center, that Nadeau’s new tax would target capital gains is risky. “This is all great when we have capital gains doing so well. But this could all go bust in a bad year. It’s very volatile,” she said. (Glen Lee, D.C.’s chief financial officer, has pointed out that one of the city’s few bright revenue spots is capital gains revenue because the stock market has been growing, though he has agreed it’s a source that is “subject to wild and sudden swings.”)

Frumin has taken a different approach, proposing his own version of New York City’s pied-à-terre tax, which targets secondary homes where the owner isn’t living on a full-time basis.

“The idea behind it is there are people who have a tax strategy which is to live in the District for one day less than six months, establish residence in a low- or no-tax state, and so they pay their property tax there and they’re here for half a year but they don’t pay income tax here. They’re employing a tax strategy, but we too have the right to employ a tax strategy to respond,” he said.

Bishop-Henchman is skeptical. “The proposal exempts members of Congress. Once you subtract those, who really is left? I would be skeptical that it would be a cash cow like NYC,” he said. Per Frumin’s office, the tax would target only 600 homeowners in D.C. and bring in an estimated $130 million over four years.

Probably the highest-profile, most lucrative and most controversial idea is a Business Activity Tax, which Lewis George has said she supports. It would take aim at law firms, consultancies and lobbying shops that are owned by nonresidents but don’t pay the city’s normal business tax because profits are treated as revenue for the owner — and Congress has prohibited D.C. from taxing nonresident income.

“The purpose of the BAT is to make sure all businesses are contributing to our shared resources, and right now there are many that are not because of the federal limitation on us,” said Erica Williams, executive director of the D.C. Fiscal Policy Institute, which favors tax increases. “A BAT helps us to broaden our tax base. That’s a good thing. That builds strength and resilience.”

Bishop-Henchman, who recently wrote an analysis of the proposed tax, questions whether it’s even legal — and notes that it would likely spur litigation. “This will be a big tax on out-of-state lawyers,” he said. In 2021, Maryland imposed a new tax on digital ads, but it was struck down this year and the state was ordered to pay refunds to those who paid the tax over the last five years.

Another challenge would be implementing a BAT. In July, the council asked the CFO to produce a report by January outlining what it would take to adopt the new tax.

Sayin believes lawmakers should focus on addressing how D.C. spends money, looking at “what drives costs, whether programs achieve their goals and which services the District can sustain.” That’s something Ward 5 council member Zachary Parker said he agrees with.

“I’ve been working to caution advocates to say that even if we were to raise taxes significantly and generated hundreds of millions of dollars, it would only keep us at pace with where we are now,” he said. “The only way we’re only going to be able to raise taxes and advance investments is by cutting our current spending. There are ways we can look at our bloated budget, look at agency spending and overspending and cut there while also making sure we fairly tax wealth.”

Still, Frumin said he appreciates the chances to broadly discuss and debate the merits and drawbacks of a number of ideas without the expectation that they will become reality soon. There’s little expectation the council would approve any tax increase this year, but it could tee something up to align with budget-writing season next spring.

Frumin also wants to proceed carefully, considering the city’s weak economy. “I will be sensitive to the possibility of different proposals driving away businesses or high-income people,” he said. “You do have to be careful of straws that break camels’ backs.”

entries.title: Nebraska Went First With Its Medicaid Cuts. Now It’s Resonating in the Midterms.
entries.summary: Work requirements that are theoretical in other states have barred more than 1,000 Nebraskans from health insurance, and Democrats are taking advantage.
entries.content:
When Republicans passed their mega tax-cut bill more than a year ago, they timed most of its more than $1 trillion in health care cuts to kick in after the midterm elections, perhaps staving off possible electoral impacts.

Nebraska, however, decided to launch early, rolling out new Medicaid work requirements in May and beginning enforcement in July, well before their mandated Jan. 1, 2027 start.

The decision turned the prospect of people losing access to health care from speculative to actual for more than 1,000 Nebraskans so far. And health care leaders, Republican observers and others now think it’s a contributor to a political climate that suddenly has GOP leaders on the defensive in a state that is reliably red.

Bob Ward, a pollster with the Republican firm Fabrizio Ward, found Medicaid cuts to be one of the most “resonating negatives” in recent surveys of rural Republicans.

“One out of two Republicans either are, have been or have a family member that is or has been on Medicaid,” Ward said, adding that the number comes from polling he conducted while Republicans were negotiating the tax bill. “I mean, it touches a lot of people or has touched a lot of people. So it's not like a theoretical thing.”

All five Nebraska Republicans in Congress backed the tax-cutting “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”, now generally referred to as HR 1, which will reduce projected Medicaid spending by about $1.2 trillion over the next decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office.The cuts are offset only by a $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Fund.

Ward’s polling observation about the Medicaid cuts is shared by people who deliver care in Nebraska, and it feeds into growing concerns about health care in the state generally, said Jeremy Nordquist, president of the Nebraska Hospital Association and a former Democratic state legislator. 

“The broader public understands the cuts that were implemented in HR 1 to Medicaid and the impact that can have,” Nordquist said. “Doesn’t matter if it’s in Omaha or it’s in western Nebraska … they know what’s coming in terms of cuts to Medicaid and what that means for our rural health care system in this state.”

Nordquist said funding for rural hospitals is particularly salient in Nebraska, where many of the institutions typically receive between 60% to 80% of their funding from government payers –– namely Medicare and Medicaid.

A study by his association found that55% of Nebraska hospitals described their financial conditions as “challenging” in January.

“It used to be this program that was kind of seen as an afterthought to Medicare, but now it's much more fundamental to the financial and health care well-being of Nebraskans,” Nordquist said. “They're much more attuned to it, and they may end up voting with Medicaid more in mind than they have before.”

Such sentiments help explain why important Republican leaders have been visiting the state, where Sen. Pete Ricketts leads his challenger, independent Dan Osborn, by just a few points. The governor’s race is also closer than many Republicans expected, with recent polls showing Gov. Jim Pillen’s lead shrinking.

Both President Donald Trump and Dr. Mehmet Oz, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services director, visited Nebraska in recent weeks, fueling speculation that Republicans are concerned about a race where Osborn often attacks Ricketts over his vote for the tax bill.

“I wouldn't have allowed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to strip a trillion dollars away from Medicaid and people's health care is going to be hurting,” Osborn said in a September debate with Ricketts, blaming the legislation for the closure of a dialysis clinic in Chadron, Nebraska.

Denise Powell, the Democrat favored to flip retiring Republican Rep. Don Bacon’s Omaha district, has also spotlighted rural health care issues, calling on Congress to reverse last year’s Medicaid cuts.

“Cutting Medicaid, raising health insurance premiums, the tariffs, the war in Iran — Brinker Harding supports Trump on all of it,” Powell says in one TV ad attacking the Omaha City Council member running on the GOP ticket

And Democratic gubernatorial nominee Lynne Walz has similarly targeted Pillen for health care spending cuts in the state, telling the Nebraska Examiner in July that “it’s going to bring about really bad outcomes in the future.”

A Ricketts loss would perhaps be the most consequential, impacting control of the Senate. His campaign told The Washington Sun that the senator has worked to protect the health care system from fraud and pointed to the funding in the Rural Health Transformation Fund as a counter to the much greater cuts. 

"He delivered $50 billion for rural healthcare,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “Dan Osborn says he would have voted against the Working Families Tax Cut. Osborn wants higher taxes on your Social Security to pay for medicaid for illegal immigrants." 

Republicans in the state have largely agreed that Democrats have successfully framed the Medicaid cuts in Nebraska, particularly as the cost of living continues to rise.

Perre Neilan, a Republican strategist, said his party has not done enough to explain the changes that were made as part of last year’s tax bill, even after Oz visited the state to discuss the rural hospital fund.

“I think Republicans have done a poor job of talking about how able-bodied men should be working,” Neilan said, referencing the new work requirements for Medicaid. “It's gotten cast as you're kicking people off health insurance and kicking people off government help.”




And Republican Ken Schilz, another former state legislator, said that although he expects health care cuts will continue to be a problem for whichever party is in power in Washington, Republicans need to find an answer on Medicaid cuts, especially while Democrats “smell blood in the water.”

“We’re seeing a lot more stress on those smaller hospitals, critical access hospitals and things like that,” Schilz said. “Rural health care was trending in this direction anyway, so something needs to change no matter what. Waiting until there’s nothing left but a crater and dust doesn’t do anything.”

entries.title: How Metro Turned L’Enfant Plaza Into a ‘Laboratory’
entries.summary: Metro uses the station as a testing ground for new wayfinding tools. Are they working?
entries.content:
The Bond family had only been in D.C. for five days, but public transit had already become a reliable resource.

The stations had been simple to navigate, Kise Bond said, and her kids had enjoyed riding the Metro. At L’Enfant Plaza, they appreciated the alphabetically coded entrances and exits.

“Just the fact that you have a Metro is amazing,” said Colton Bond, who was holding on to his family’s luggage as they waited for a Silver Line train to be whisked away toward their flight back to Salem, Oregon.

But the Bonds didn’t know they were joining the 14,000 other daily entrants at L’Enfant in one big experiment.

For the last three years, L’Enfant Plaza has been the hub for the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority’s trials and tests on the Metro system’s signage. Officials refer to it as the system’s “live laboratory.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Conveniently located next to Metro’s headquarters and just a short walk from the National Mall, the agency has simulated the station in virtual reality, used it to launch numerous sign iterations — ranging from bright, real-time digital station displays to minimalist Helvetica text above the third rail — and recently selected it as the first to receive updates as part of its $37.8 million wayfinding program.

After a 2023 study found that 39% of Metro passengers had used the wrong station exit and 23% had boarded a train headed in the wrong direction, testing at L’Enfant began as a process to consolidate signage across the system and improve accessibility, Brian Anderson, Metro’s acting vice president for customer experience initiatives, told The Washington Sun during a tour of the station. The agency has between 20 and 25 different sign types across its 98 active stations, Anderson said. The hope is to get that number down to just 10 to 15.

But while some of the pilot program’s sign changes were small, even incremental, the rollout of the wayfinding program has created the most customer heartburn so far.

Online, riders have expressed dismay about the new signs, describing them as “not well done” or “Metro enshitification.” The pushback to one proposed change — removing stripes around pylons outside of Metro stops — led WMATA to reverse course.

From old to new, signs on the walls of Metro stations will no longer include route endpoints indicating direction, and some signs, like those on platforms or near exits, will include points of interest like airports or the National Zoo. All signs hanging above third rails have more negative space, a minimalist design choice that has come with an updated medium-weight Helvetica font. Exits will no longer be labeled by street but by letters.
_MG_3957 copy 2.jpg (5710x3807, AR: 1.50)Importantly, no signs will include cardinal directions, a change made to increase accessibility and reflect that not all lines, like the U-shaped Red Line, follow linear directions. Within the next five years, all stations are expected to have the new signage, Metro said.

Cleaning up visual clutter — like reducing the number of names, arrows and colors on signs — will likely decrease the chance that users are confused in stations, said Jihyun Song, a wayfinding researcher who takes the Silver Line on her way to work at George Washington University.

But some changes, particularly the removal of directions from wall signs, may leave customers confused, Song said.

Laura Heatherly, who is visually impaired and uses a mobility cane to navigate, said the removal of directional indicators had actually made determining which train she’s waiting for at L’Enfant more difficult.

“I can normally look at a sign and easily find my way around, but now I can’t tell which one is going north or south. I usually have to ask around,” Heatherly, a frequent L’Enfant user, said while waiting on the Green-Yellow Line platform.

In some ways, the removal of information reflects a return to the ethos of the original design of the Metro and highlights an ongoing “special tension” between the agency’s aesthetics and the public, said Zachary Schrag, the author of “The Great Society Subway: A History of the Washington Metro.”
_MG_3905 copy 2.jpg (5490x3660, AR: 1.50)With fights about signage dating back to 1976, the battle over Metro aesthetics is as old as the system itself, Schrag said. Other battles have taken place over lighting or paint along the vault walls of Metro stops.

“People do get fussy about changes. I think one of the differences with this most recent wayfinding effort is that it was more deliberate and more public,” said Schrag, a professor of U.S. history at George Mason University. Before unveiling the changes, WMATA received over 13,000 comments on Metro signage, and the final product was approved by its Accessibility Advisory Committee, its Riders’ Advisory Committee and the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts.

“You cannot always appeal 100% to every single person,” said Anderson, who at one point stopped to offer a customer directions during the tour. “But we are very confident in what we have delivered, and we appreciate the feedback.”

Still, some riders are oblivious to the L’Enfant laboratory.

Just before a recent afternoon rush hour, Leroy Ferguson said he hadn’t noticed the new minimalist text hanging over the third rail. A D.C. resident for 15 years, Ferguson uses the Metro every day. When he sees lost tourists, he offers them simple advice.

“Always follow the signs,” he said. “Always follow the signs.”

entries.title: FIFA Is Deciding on the Future of the Peace Prize It Gave to Trump
entries.summary: Gianni Infantino, FIFA’s president, gave Trump the award last December without going through the organization's decision-making body.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump could go down as the sole winner of the FIFA Peace Prize.

On Thursday, the FIFA Council met in Zurich and decided that the social responsibility committee for soccer’s governing body will be assigned with evaluating the award, which was supposed to be handed out annually.

“There’s a decision taken to look at the peace prize and to take that through the social committee,” FIFA vice president Debbie Hewitt told reporters following Thursday’s meeting. “That was another issue that was raised: whether there should have been one, how the decision was taken to award it, and whether there should be another one. And those questions will be answered through the social committee.”

FIFA president Gianni Infantino gave Trump, who has long sought the Nobel Peace Prize, the award last December before the U.S. hosted the 2026 World Cup along with Canada and Mexico. Infantino named Trump the winner without going through the FIFA Council, which is the organization's decision-making body.

The award was first announced in November 2025, a month before Trump was named the winner. At the time, FIFA said it would be an annual prize to “reward individuals who have taken exceptional and extraordinary actions for peace.” Article 2 of FIFA’s statutes prohibit political and government interference in football, which contributed to the backlash the governing body received after Trump won it.

The social responsibility committee consists of 22 people and is chaired by U Zaw Zaw, the senior vice president of the Asian Football Confederation, and includes former Argentinian star Javier Zanetti, who is its deputy chairperson.

The committee has a range of options. It could discontinue the award, make politicians ineligible to win it, or hand it out less frequently. The next FIFA Council meeting is scheduled for Dec. 16 in Doha, Qatar. A decision from the social responsibility committee is expected to be made in time for the meeting.

entries.title: The National Zoo Is Asking the Public to Name Its Red Panda Cub
entries.summary: The cub with a coat of many colors could be named after Dolly Parton.
entries.content:
The Smithsonian’s National Zoo is asking the public to vote on one of three name options for a red panda cub, including one that pays homage to the Queen of Country.

The cub was born in June at a conservation campus in Front Royal, Virginia, to 3-year-old female Keahi and 7-year-old male Rocket.

The 4-month-old female cub has already “distinguished herself with bold and feisty behavior,” officials said. Still, the cub is unnamed, and the zoo is looking for help deciding what to call her.

The three name candidates are “Pyra,” which the zoo says means “heat” in Greek, “Dolpa,” a region of Nepal home to wild red pandas, and “Dolly,” inspired by country music legend Dolly Parton.

Two weeks before the cub’s birth, two other red panda cubs were born on the campus. Since the births, keepers and staff have closely monitored the three. Red pandas generally have low survival rates, the zoo said in the birth announcement.

“The cubs are really just balls of fur that eat and sleep right now,” said Jessica Kordell, assistant curator of carnivores, in an August news release.

The public can cast their ballots online until Saturday, and the winning name will be announced shortly after.

entries.title: Kristi Noem Is Out of a Job Once Again
entries.summary: Noem was appointed to a role as special envoy to the Shield of the Americas initiative shortly after her tenure at DHS ended.
entries.content:
Kristi Noem is no longer serving as special envoy to the Shield of the Americas, the State Department announced this week.

The former homeland security secretary was appointed to the position in March after a brief tenure at the department, which was marred in controversy.

"Kristi Noem's envoy status expired last month and she is no longer in the role," a State Department spokesperson told The Washington Sun. "She is now a senior advisor to Deputy Secretary Landau and continues to work on the Shield of the Americas portfolio."

The Trump administration launched the coalition in March. It’s tasked with advancing strategies that stop foreign interference in the Western Hemisphere.

The coalition is composed of the U.S., Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago.

Noem concluded her role at DHS earlier this year and began her new post by traveling to Costa Rica to sign a cooperation agreement facilitating the transfer of third-country nationals ordered removed from the U.S., according to a news release.

Noem also traveled to Guyana and the Dominican Republic as part of her special envoy role.

The former secretary’s time at Homeland Security was fraught with controversy.

She’d been accused of using $200 million in taxpayer dollars for an ad campaign featuring herself on horseback in front of Mount Rushmore.

She’d also been scrutinized over her handling of the department after federal agents fatally shot two U.S. citizens in Minneapolis, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti.

Corey Lewandowski, who had an unpaid role as the department’s “special government employee” and was her right-hand man, was also accused of attempting to profit from government contracts.

Lewandowski has denied the allegations.

Noem was fired the day after she appeared before the House Judiciary Committee at an oversight hearing. While being questioned, she referred to Good and Pretti as “domestic terrorists” and declined to apologize to their families.

entries.title: Trump Fires His New Press Secretary After Disastrous First Week
entries.summary: Zacharia was beleaguered by bad headlines and questions about her qualifications from the start of her five-day tenure.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump has fired Katie Zacharia from her post as White House press secretary after less than a week on the job, according to a source familiar with the matter.

It’s a stunning exit for Zacharia, who had been beleaguered by bad headlines and questions about her qualifications from the start of her five-day tenure.

Trump foreshadowed the exit on Friday, telling reporters that he asked her to consider stepping aside after a difficult first week on the job.

Trump announced her appointment in a Truth Social post last Friday, and she assumed the position on Monday — but a widely panned first press conference and a series of awkward interviews left the president questioning her ability to perform the strenuous job of speaking for the commander-in-chief.

“Katie has been treated very badly by the media. Very, very badly. Very unfair,” Trump said. “I just asked her, is this for you? And she's a nice person. I'm going to let her make that decision.”

When asked whether she would remain in the administration if ousted, Trump replied, “In some form.”

“But maybe a more pleasant form,” he added.

Fox News was the first of multiple outlets to report her ouster following Trump’s comments.

Trump didn’t drop names when asked who her successor could be, but he told a reporter: “A lot of people want the job. I bet you’d want it if I offered it to you.”

Controversy surrounding Zacharia’s legal credentials became a focal point this week after Popular Information reported that Zacharia, a California resident, has never been admitted to practice law in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia.

Zacharia herself confirmed she hadn’t passed the bar in a viral interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity. 

“You took the bar exam but you didn’t pass the bar exam, correct?” Hannity asked her. 

“Yes, Sean,” she answered. Hannity then asked her if she took the bar a second time, and she responded she did not. 

Despite this, Zacharia repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer when appearing on podcasts and on TV. Zacharia told The New York Times she decided to publicly refer to herself as an attorney after consulting with Pepperdine University’s president. 

The university president warned her not to use the words “attorney” or “esquire,” but said “lawyer” was permissible, the Times reported. 

On her LinkedIn page, Zacharia also identified herself as former general counsel to Fix California, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting conservative values across the state, and as a former associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013.

The Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the California State Bar on Wednesday over allegations that Zacharia had misrepresented herself as an attorney. 

As the music played out on Hannity, Zacharia continued trying to assure the host she’d deliver for the president. 

“I’ll be very prepared, Sean, and I’ll step up to the duty … as press secretary.”

The morning after her Hannity interview, a former Trump official sent The Washington Sun a link to a Polymarket X post, unprompted and without context. Zacharia’s odds to be fired had increased by 12%.

A current administration official only had one word for her performance with the typically friendly Hannity: “Wow.” He continued: “Let's get someone serious now."

entries.title: Trump Again Bars CNN From Accessing Air Force One
entries.summary: The network was scheduled to cover President Donald Trump’s travels to Florida and Georgia this weekend.
entries.content:
The White House again barred CNN from its traveling television pool Friday, preventing the network from accompanying President Donald Trump aboard Air Force One amid a legal battle over press access.

CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter said the network was scheduled to provide footage for other major networks from Friday to Sunday as Trump visits Georgia and Florida this weekend, including coverage of his campaign appearances and time at Mar-a-Lago.

“Once again, there will not be pooled TV coverage of the president’s appearances,” Stelter wrote on X. The disruption affects other news outlets worldwide.

Earlier this week, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly extended an order protecting White House access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico while their lawsuit against the administration proceeds. But that ruling does not settle access for reporters whose duty it is to travel with the president on Air Force One.

That issue remains the subject of separate litigation involving The Associated Press.

The Washington Sun has signed on to an amicus brief in support of the news outlets.

entries.title: Democrats Are Bringing in Elizabeth Warren to Close Their Affordability Pitch
entries.summary: The senator said she’s making the case that Democrats need control of Congress to pass more housing legislation.
entries.content:
Democrats are using Sen. Elizabeth Warren as a surrogate to close on their affordability message in the final weeks of the campaign.

Warren will appear in Maine, Nevada and New Mexico in the coming days to make the case that electing candidates there will help Democrats address the high costs of housing and goods.

“[Voters] want their elected officials to hear how hard it is for them, and they want to hear real plans about what candidates will do if they get elected,” Warren said in an interview with The Washington Sun ahead of a campaign event Thursday with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.

Democrats nationwide have focused their election message on affordability, for good reason: 84% of voters cited the cost of living as a top issue in their midterm vote, according to an AP-NORC poll conducted in October.

Warren is scheduled to campaign Saturday with Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson in Maine. On Monday, she’s expected to join former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, who is running to become the next governor of New Mexico, before campaigning in Nevada alongside Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, who has organized visits to the state for her Senate colleagues.

“I couldn't miss a chance to go to Nevada, partly to make sure that everyone in the state knows about the work [Cortez Masto]’s done to lower housing costs, and partly to say thank you.” Warren said.

Warren will appear with Nevada Reps. Susie Lee and Dina Titus, as well as Democratic gubernatorial nominee Aaron Ford, who’s challenging Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. The race for governor in the state is currently ranked as a toss-up by The Cook Political Report.

She has also campaigned for Senate Democratic nominees Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire and Juliana Stratton of Illinois, as well as incumbent Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff. As of August, Warren has donated $600,000 to Democrats ahead of the midterm elections.

Warren’s message on the campaign trail is that electing more Democrats to Congress and state offices would help advance their plans to ease costs on housing and other goods.

The housing bill she pushed through earlier this year — the first to come out of Congress in more than three decades — is a key component of her midterm message. The housing package became law in July even though the president refused to sign it despite previously endorsing it.

“We're already underway with Road to Housing 2.0, but with lots of room to expand,” Warren said. “Housing is the single biggest expense that most families ever take on, and housing is becoming so expensive that first-time homebuyers see home ownership as out of reach.”

If Democrats controlled the House and Senate, they would push for new housing legislation focused on “starter homes, renters, and manufactured housing,” Warren said.

Cortez Masto echoed Warren’s pitch for electing Democrats in order to enact more housing legislation.

“I am proud of the work Senator Warren and I did,” Cortez Masto told The Sun in a statement. “In a Democratic Congress, I look forward to ensuring the ROAD to Housing Act is implemented… and fighting back against the Trump Administration and big corporations if they try to stall it.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump is “laser-focused” on lowering housing costs and “will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American.”

Warren doesn’t buy it, as she tells voters when she speaks to them.

“Donald Trump calls affordability a hoax and says lowering housing costs is a big yawn,” she said. “Trump promised he would lower costs on day one … the cost of groceries, housing, electricity bills, gas prices.”

entries.title: A Texas Republican Wants a Billboard Featuring Trump's Endorsement to Come Down
entries.summary: A lawyer for Eric Flores, who is running in a competitive House district, sent a cease and desist over a billboard it argues could “cause voter confusion.”
entries.content:
A billboard in Brownsville, Texas, featuring Republican congressional candidate Eric Flores so closely resembles his campaign ads it could be one of his campaign posters.

Except unlike his campaign posters, it prominently features an endorsement by and photo of Flores with President Donald Trump, which Democrats are now accusing Flores of trying to bury. The billboard also touts his “support” of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In an Oct. 12 cease-and-desist letter obtained by The Washington Sun, attorney Eric Wang, who represents the Flores campaign, demanded that Lamar Advertising of the Rio Grande Valley, the billboard company that put it up, immediately remove the digital billboard.

Wang alleged in the cease-and-desist letter that the advertisement is designed to confuse voters into believing it is an official campaign message.

“The Billboard intentionally mimics the distinctive look of our client’s campaign signs and other materials to cause voter confusion,” the letter states. “The Billboard’s intent to deceive voters is unmistakable.”

The letter says the sign “fraudulently purports to be on behalf of” the Flores campaign. Across the bottom, it says it was paid for by the campaign of Rep. Vicente Gonzalez — the incumbent Democratic lawmaker running for reelection in the battleground district.

Trump did back Flores in December, saying he has his “complete and total endorsement” in a Truth Social post.

The cease-and-desist letter names the Northern Cameron County Democrats as the group that paid for the billboard, even though the billboard says it was paid for by Gonzalez’s campaign. NCC Democrats did not respond to a request for comment.

Lamar Advertising did not respond to a request for comment about the letter. The Gonzalez campaign told The Sun that as of Friday, the billboard is still up.

Flores’ campaign confirmed the authenticity of the cease-and-desist letter but disputed that it had anything to do with the Trump endorsement or the listed support of ICE.

"Vicente Gonzalez is a practiced scammer who has been running a con on South Texas voters for years. This billboard is just the most recent example,” Matt Brownfield, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. “It is designed, on purpose, to cause people to think that it comes from the Flores Campaign. It is deceptive on its face. It is a scam.”

The letter does not explicitly dispute that Trump endorsed Flores or that Flores supports ICE. The legal argument in the letter focuses on the billboard's appearance and the possibility that voters could mistake it for an advertisement authorized by the Flores campaign.

The Texas Observer reported earlier this month that Flores' campaign signs no longer prominently advertise Trump's endorsement like they did during the primary. Instead, Flores campaign materials emphasize his biography and professional background.

That’s part of a broader trend of Republicans purging their campaign materials of mentions of Trump across the country, where GOP candidates are coping with the administration’s low approval ratings and affordability issues.

It also comes as candidates compete for voters in a South Texas congressional district where immigration, border security and the president's political standing are prominent issues. The district was redrawn after Trump captured the majority of the vote in the district in the 2024 election, making it one of the most competitive districts in the country.

Gonzalez's campaign accused Flores of attempting to distance himself from positions he had previously embraced.

“Eric Flores proudly bragged about his Trump endorsement during the primary. Now he’s ashamed and is trying to distance himself from the President and the hyperaggressive ICE raids devastating our economy, but voters see right through his charade and deserve to know the truth,” a campaign spokesperson said in a statement. “If Eric truly feels this billboard is misleading, he should’ve met Congressman Gonzalez on the debate stage to explain his positions to voters. Instead, he walked away at the last minute because he couldn’t bend the rules in his favor.”

Like Gonzalez’s campaign, BOLD PAC, the Congressional Hispanic Caucus’ campaign arm, characterized the cease-and-desist letter as trying to hide the endorsement.

“Eric Flores bragged about Trump's endorsement until South Texas saw what it cost them: higher prices and ICE in our neighborhoods,” Valeria Ojeda-Avitia, a spokesperson for BOLD PAC, said in a statement. “Now he's paying lawyers to hide it.”

entries.title: Amtrak Closes Route Between Alexandria and Union Station Until Oct. 26
entries.summary: The railroad company said track switches between the stations are beyond their service life, making phased construction impractical.
entries.content:
Commuters who regularly ride Amtrak between Virginia and D.C. will have to reroute until Oct. 26 due to a closure for a “critical” infrastructure upgrade.

After service ends Friday night, work will begin inside the First Street Tunnel south of Union Station, closing trips to and from Alexandria.

During the closure, Amtrak will provide three round-trip buses between Alexandria and Union Station, along with several express bus routes connecting passenger rail service stops to the District.

Amtrak also suggests on its website that riders take the D.C. Metrorail Yellow or Blue lines from the King Street-Old Town station, a short walk from the Alexandria Amtrak station, to reach D.C. during the improvements.

The work, called the “Pause for Progress” project, was announced in late August. It will replace track components and improve reliability at the “A-Interlocking” track control point between the two stations.

“The existing switches and crossovers are beyond their service life, requiring a 10-mph speed restriction that impacts operations,” an Amtrak news release said. “A short-term, coordinated outage is more efficient due to the confined tunnel environment and limited access, making phased construction impractical.”

A spokesperson with the Virginia Passenger Rail Authority, which operates the Amtrak Virginia route in partnership with Amtrak, told The Washington Sun the line between Alexandria and Union Station is vital to its service and that nearly 600,000 passengers used the tunnel to travel between Virginia and the Northeast last year.

“All of our trains travel through the tunnel when arriving and departing Union Station, and approximately 40% of our passengers connect to Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, so access to Union Station is necessary,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Amtrak did not respond to a request for further comment.

entries.title: ‘Unknown Actors’ Attempted to Steal Tens of Thousands From Iowa Candidate
entries.summary: It’s the latest in a string of thefts and theft attempts to hit federal political committees.
entries.content:
“Unknown actors” twice targeted Iowa state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott in attempts to steal tens of thousands of dollars from the Democrat’s congressional campaign committee, according to a new letter from the campaign to the Federal Election Commission.

One attempted theft happened on Aug. 6, when the Sarah for Iowa campaign initiated a $48,568.16 electronic payment to a vendor. Soon after, “an external actor altered the invoice in an attempt to redirect the payment to another bank account,” the Trone Garriott campaign told the FEC.

The campaign spotted the attempted theft two days later and “notified law enforcement when the police station opened the next day, obtaining a police report.” The campaign also “alerted the recipient bank, which flagged the transaction.”

The money never made it to the would-be thieves, and the campaign later paid the vendor via check.

About two months later, on Oct. 8, the campaign discovered a separate incident after a “vendor resubmitted a $15,000 invoice the Committee believed it had paid on June 16.” The campaign notified the police that day and repaid the vendor on Oct. 14. It’s unclear whether the campaign lost any or all of the $15,000.

Theresa Kehoe, Trone Garriott’s campaign treasurer, declined to comment, and another campaign official could not be reached for comment. The Des Moines Police Department also could not be reached for comment.

Trone Garriott has raised roughly $7.5 million in her bid to unseat Republican Rep. Zach Nunn in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, which was recently rated “leans Democrat” by The Cook Political Report.

The campaign said in its letter to the FEC that it “has strengthened its payment-verification procedures to prevent similar unauthorized activity.”

Numerous federal political committees have experienced incidents involving theft or embezzlement this decade.

Earlier this month, The Washington Sun reported that Citizens Against AIPAC Corruption, the Democratic Party of Oregon and the political action committee for power company Pinnacle West Capital Corporation each fell victim to fraudsters.

In July, the PAC tied to the law firm Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer LLP told federal regulators that some political contribution checks had been stolen from mailboxes in D.C., and the thieves altered the values of the paper checks. The law firm said it recouped the stolen funds, which amounted to $40,000.

That same month, The Sun reported that the Democratic National Committee had been scammed out of nearly $29,000 in February 2025 after a staffer received an email from someone pretending to be the newly elected DNC Chair Ken Martin.

In August, the National Republican Congressional Committee said an unknown actor stole more than $16,300 that was intended for a vendor. The NRCC told The Sun that it was working with the authorities to recoup the funds.

Political committees for Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) and accounting giant KPMG have also been hit by thieves in recent months.

entries.title: Two Republican Senate Hopefuls Are Running Out of Cash
entries.summary: Battleground candidates in Georgia and North Carolina are watching their odds dwindle as money evaporates.
entries.content:
In North Carolina and Georgia, Democratic Senate candidates are lapping their Republican rivals in fundraising, according to new campaign finance reports.

It’s the latest ominous sign for Michael Whatley and Mike Collins, the Republican candidates who have seen national party attention shift to other races amid attempts to win enough seats to retain a Senate majority.

North Carolina’s Whatley raised $13.4 million during the two-year 2026 election cycle. His Democratic opponent, Roy Cooper, raised nearly that much money in just the three-month period from July to September — and $47 million overall for the cycle.

Cooper ended September with $12.5 million on hand. Whatley ended September with about $900,000 on hand, according to FEC records.

Cooper has consistently led Whatley in polling. Earlier this month, Republicans’ Senate Leadership Fund super PAC shifted funds from North Carolina to races in Kansas and South Carolina, and Whatley’s own campaign committee does not have any TV ads reserved.

In Georgia, Collins has raised just $5.8 million this election cycle through Sept. 30 — a tiny fraction of the nearly $125 million incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has raised.

Ossoff raised $33 million from July through September and entered October armed with $26 million ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3.
Election 2026 Georgia Ossoff (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Collins raised $2.8 million during the same three-month span and had only $1.1 million on hand entering October.

As in North Carolina, Ossoff has consistently led in Georgia polls, and national PACs aligned with both parties have pulled spending out — a sign they view an Ossoff victory as a fait accompli.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund shifted nearly $2 million from Georgia to South Carolina, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s Senate Majority PAC removed ad spending it had reserved for this week.

Thune’s Senate Leadership Fund finished September with $155 million on hand, while Schumer’s Senate Majority PAC reported $112 million.

Thune’s PAC is spending heavily in Alaska, Maine and Texas.

In Texas, Republican Ken Paxton, the party’s Senate nominee, is being supported by more than $150 million in super PAC cash from Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. Paxton’s own campaign raised $10.3 million from July 1 through Sept. 30 and had $4.9 million on hand going into October.

Democrat James Talarico’s campaign committee raised $60 million during the same period, bringing his fundraising total for the cycle to nearly $129 million. Talarico’s campaign began October with $14.6 million on hand, according to FEC records.

entries.title: Israeli Settlers Beat a Washington Post Photographer in a West Bank Attack
entries.summary: The perpetrators “were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag,” photographer Heidi Levine said.
entries.content:
By Sam Metz and Leo Correa

Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank on Friday, setting fire to cars and trees and beating residents and a Washington Post photographer, in the latest violence to disrupt the territory's annual olive harvest this month.

Settlers attacked the village as residents, accompanied by peace activists, set out early for the harvest.

As the group of masked vigilantes approached, several members beat Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was hospitalized for her injuries.

The perpetrators — armed with bottles and slingshots — “were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag,” Levine said.

Levine said her helmet and protective vest, which was marked “PRESS,” likely saved her from more serious injuries.

Israel’s military on Friday condemned the violence and acknowledged that a journalist was injured in Abu Falah.

Both the Washington Post and the Foreign Press Association, which represents international journalists working in Israel and the Palestinian territories, called on Israel to bring the attackers to justice.

“This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," the Foreign Press Association said.

The U.S. State Department said that “we condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible,” adding that it has reached out to The Washington Post to offer consular assistance.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has repeatedly framed settler violence in the West Bank as the work of a few dozen fringe youths and said its scale has been exaggerated.

He condemned the violence in Abu Falah on Friday but questioned whether Palestinians and activists were to blame. Without mentioning accounts of how the attacking settlers descended on the groves, he framed the violence as a clash between outnumbered Israeli youths against Palestinians and activists.

“We will not allow disputed incidents to be exploited to demonize the hundreds of thousands of law-abiding Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria,” his office said in a statement, referring to the West Bank by the biblical name preferred by Israeli settlers.

entries.title: AOC Puts $1 Million Behind El-Sayed in High-Stakes Michigan Senate Race
entries.summary: Her campaign holds nearly $17.4 million in cash on hand, recent financial disclosures show.
entries.content:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez transferred $1 million to Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign on Friday, using her significant cash reserves to boost a battleground Senate race in Michigan as the party aims to regain control of the chamber.

Ocasio-Cortez has become a financial engine, handily outraising even top Senate Democrats this election cycle. The investment comprises roughly 6% of her campaign’s coffers — an unusually large sum coming from a House member from a different state. The New York congresswoman will stump with El-Sayed in Detroit this weekend.

She fronted the money so she wouldn’t have to wake up on Nov. 4 “wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” she told The New York Times Friday.

“I’m leaving everything I can on the field,” she said.

Her committee transferred the funds to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, a joint fundraising committee involving El-Sayed’s campaign, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Michigan Democratic State Central Committee, according to the Times.

Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign reported having nearly $17.4 million in cash on hand as of Sept. 30 after raising $4.7 million last quarter.

El-Sayed is facing former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in a race that has drummed up $181 million in advertising spending, according to AdImpact.

The Michigan progressive’s candidacy will prove consequential for Congress’ burgeoning left-wing movement, which is in part led by Ocasio-Cortez in the House and Vermont independent Bernie Sanders in the Senate. At a recent New York fundraiser, she framed El-Sayed’s solid chances as evidence that progressives can compete nationally.

Ocasio-Cortez has declined to rule out running for president in 2028 — laughing off a question about it while in Michigan Friday — or challenging the Senate’s top Democrat, Chuck Schumer, for his seat. The representative is expected to easily defeat her Republican challenger, Diamant Hysenaj, in November.

entries.title: ACA Premiums Will Rise by Double Digits for the Second Year in a Row
entries.summary: The health insurance costs won’t spike as badly as last year but will still rise 11%, per documents provided to The Washington Sun.
entries.content:
Costs for health insurance plans sold on Healthcare.gov will rise by double digits next year, and Americans will have access to fewer insurers, according to government documents reviewed by The Washington Sun.

Average monthly premiums for the most popular types of plans will increase 11% in 2027. While prices are increasing, the jump is not as dramatic as last year, when costs shot up by 30% — a sign the federal health insurance marketplaces covering 19 million Americans are on more stable footing even as costs continue to rise.

“It’s not great news but it’s also not a collapse,” said Cynthia Cox, a senior vice president at nonpartisan health policy organization KFF, who tracks the Affordable Care Act closely.

The documents also showed a significant exodus of insurers from the marketplaces. In 2027, there will be 152 insurers on Healthcare.gov, down 14% from this year. Major insurer Cigna announced earlier this year it would withdraw from marketplaces in all the states. The average enrollee will still have access to plans from five or six insurers.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services is expected to release the figures ahead of the start of open enrollment on Nov. 1 and just before a midterm election where Democrats are hammering Republicans over the chronic problem of high health care costs.

The Trump administration has been striving to portray Healthcare.gov plans as affordable but last month announced it’s sending $500 checks to nearly 1 million marketplace customers who earn too much to qualify for premium subsidies.

The checks — which President Donald Trump called a “historic action” — will help defray but won’t entirely cover the premium increases for most consumers, depending on which plan they choose. According to the CMS documents, an average, midlevel “silver” plan will cost $73 more a month, or $876 more a year. Customers can also buy more expensive gold plans with more benefits or cheaper bronze plans with fewer benefits.

CMS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The figures only reflect the 29 states relying on Healthcare.gov rather than running their own marketplaces. The marketplaces were created by President Barack Obama’s 2010 health care law for Americans who don’t have insurance through their employer, Medicare or Medicaid. Customers can buy individual health plans using federal subsidies pegged to their income.

For years, Democrats defended the health care law as Republicans vowed to repeal and replace it. But the script flipped last year after congressional Republicans refused to extend pandemic-era subsidies that were expiring.

Marketplace insurers had already indicated they planned a second year of double-digit rate hikes in filings with states earlier this year. The median premium increase across all 50 states and the District of Columbia will be 15%, according to a preliminary analysis by KFF.

Most marketplace customers are eligible for federal subsidies, which in many cases dramatically reduce their monthly premium costs, especially if they buy a bronze plan. Like last year, the subsidies will cover 88%, on average, of the premium for the lowest-cost plan, according to the CMS documents.

Marketplace enrollment declined by several million this year as premiums spiked to their highest levels since 2018. Insurers blamed the increases partly on the loss of the extra subsidies, along with growing drug and hospital costs and medical inflation.

entries.title: Trump Critic Stephen A. Smith Has Dinner at the White House
entries.summary: Smith and Trump have traded public jabs this year, with the president calling him an “arrogant fool” and a “low IQ individual.”
entries.content:
Stephen A. Smith, the longtime sports commentator and recent critic of President Donald Trump, reportedly joined the president for dinner at the White House alongside musician Kid Rock and comedian Bill Maher on Thursday.

Trump confirmed the dinner happened while speaking to the White House press corps on Friday. 

“The dinner last night with Kid Rock, Stephen A. and Bill Maher was great,” said Trump. “I think they had a good time.”

He added: “Stephen A. is great. Bill Maher, I’ll tell you what, he likes me a lot more than people understand, and I actually like him.”

Kid Rock dished about the gathering while speaking to Fox News on Friday, saying it was “epic.”

“Two Democrats, two Republicans sit down, break bread, have laughs, have tough conversations on a lot of the issues,” said Kid Rock, noting the group discussed “everything from socialism and communism to the war in Iran.”

Smith and Maher both publicly identify as Democrats, and one of the few things the group agreed on was that “socialism and communism [have] no place to have a foothold in our government,” Kid Rock said.

The musician and comedian both had dinner with the president at the White House last year.

But it appears this was Smith’s first time meeting Trump at the White House.

During the dinner, Smith apparently discussed unemployment among Black women and funding for historically Black colleges and universities. Kid Rock recalled Smith telling the president that corporations have been discouraged from donating to the institutions after Trump put a “dagger through the heart of DEI.”

The musician said he spoke for the president when he told the show hosts, “We want to encourage corporations to continue funding HBCUs and donating to them because we know how important education is … to strengthening Black families.”

Smith is weighing a 2028 presidential bid, the sports analyst told CBS Sunday Morning earlier this year.

“I think that the American people deserve to listen to and hear from somebody who genuinely cares about making life better for them,” he told the program, Deadline reported.

Smith has taken issue with the president in the past. Days before Trump was set to attend Game 3 of this year’s NBA Finals at Madison Square Garden, Smith criticized the president and said his presence could cause delays and interfere with watch parties across New York City.

After Smith’s remarks, the president called him an “arrogant fool” and a “low IQ individual” in a Truth Social post. “Totally unqualified to ever think of running for high political office.”

Smith continued the beef on his SiriusXM Sports Show, stating he’d “smoke” Trump in a debate “any time, any place, anywhere.”

Maher has similarly been an outspoken critic of the president but has notably softened his tone since Trump returned to office last year.

Maher confirmed he’d be attending this week’s dinner while speaking on an episode of his “Club Random” podcast released Monday.

At the gathering, he discussed bringing Afghan interpreters who worked alongside U.S. military and government forces to the U.S., Kid Rock said.

In April, The New York Times reported Trump was in talks to relocate approximately 1,100 Afghans who assisted in the war to the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Maher said the president invited him to dinner “out of the blue” following last year’s meal.

The comedian described the president as “really nice” and said the commander-in-chief promised not to say bad things about him.

Maher texted back: “You know what, you’re the president of the United States …I’m just glad we’re talking.”
