entries.title: Could Trump Sell Presidential Records on eBay? DOJ Doesn’t Say No.
entries.summary: Attorney argues the Trump administration is concerned with the next president embarrassing the current White House.
entries.content:
The Trump administration told an appellate court Friday that a president could do whatever he wants with records that include the nation's most guarded secrets — and potentially even sell them on eBay.

John Bailey, a Justice Department attorney, argued that the 1978 Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional, a conclusion the department made in April. The post-Watergate law says that all official records created or received by presidents are U.S. government property.

Judge Patricia Millett summed up the DOJ’s argument by focusing on how it would impact not just the current president, but the institution of the Executive Office of the President, which she referred to as the EOP.

“You have adopted a position that says the president, whoever it is at the time, on Jan 20th can take every record — every record within the EOP — and destroy it so that the incoming president has no information about national security threats, about planned terrorist attacks, about critical negotiations in an ongoing war, critical economic negotiations for the health of this country's economy ... has to come in knowing nothing. You have said that is what the Constitution requires in your view,” Millett said.

Bailey replied: “Our position is that, yes, because the Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional.”

He didn’t back down, even when Millett tossed out an extreme hypothetical. “Can the president then offer on eBay to sell them, all of our national security secrets, to the highest bidder? They're his property,” she said. “Can he?”

Bailey stammered at first, but eventually replied, “The Presidential Records Act is unconstitutional would not be a bar to that —”

“Your argument is that these records are his property, correct?” Millett interrupted.

“Consistent with history and tradition, yes,” Bailey said.

“I'm not asking you the source of your argument. I'm asking you your argument. These are his property to do with as he likes, correct?”

“The president's papers belong to the president, yes,” Bailey asserted.

The arguments came in a legal challenge brought by a watchdog group and historians who fear the wholesale destruction of records when the second Trump administration ends in just over two years.

Congress passed the PRA in the shadow of the Watergate scandal after two centuries of presidents laying claim to their official records. President Richard Nixon stepped down but later sought to assert ownership of White House tapes that documented his misconduct in office.

Trump already has a thorny relationship with the PRA, because of the way he removed classified government records from the White House upon his exit in 2021 and relocated them to his oceanside mansion of Mar-a-Lago when he was a regular citizen. He faced criminal charges related to the records until a judge, whom Trump himself appointed, dismissed the indictment during the height of Trump’s re-election campaign in 2024.

The April opinion from DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel, which issues executive branch legal guidance but has no constitutional authority, reversed course on nearly 50 years of White House administrations abiding by the PRA.

The 52-page memo, signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser, a Trump appointee who once interned at the conservative Heritage Foundation, concluded that the law mandating public access to presidential records “serves no identifiable and valid legislative purpose.”

“It exceeds any preservation power because Congress cannot preserve presidential records merely for the sake of posterity,” the memo says.

American Oversight and the American Historical Association sued the next week. In May, U.S. District Judge John Bates temporarily blocked the Trump administration from abiding by the new DOJ legal guidance — essentially ensuring the White House continues to abide by the PRA. The administration appealed the ruling, which led to Friday’s hearing.

At the arguments, DOJ said part of the concern was an attempt to prevent the next presidential administration from exposing internal records that would embarrass Trump.

The revelation was made when the DOJ’s lawyer was arguing about why the current administration would want to control the flow of information to the next president — and the notion that Congress could try to pass a narrower version of the PRA with new restrictions.

“Your honor, if the [next] president’s ideas of his official duties is posting his predecessor’s advisers’ communications to embarrass them for political gain, we think that's a problem,” Bailey said.

The comment drew a sarcastic response from Millett, who said: “Oh! It's going to be a motive test! We’re going to have a motive test the afternoon of January 20th? That's what you want: Is this for good reasons or this is to embarrass a past president? That's the test Congress is supposed to write into the law?”

Bailey doubled down on that rationale in a later exchange with Judge Cornelia T.L. Pillard, who once worked as a senior attorney at the DOJ office that issued the new memo.

He stressed that “giving control to a future president” was the primary concern here. “That is the very issue,” Bailey argued. “It is that loss of control that is impairing the executive branch's ability ... to get candid advice from advisers.”

Pillard said: “That is such a sad and such a partisan view, assuming that the separation of powers doesn't protect the office of the presidency but only this president. And it's just never been the case.”

In a call after the court hearing with both advocacy organizations, American Oversight Executive Deputy Director Liz Hempowicz addressed that exchange.

“I don’t think there's anything in the Constitution about embarrassing the executive,” she said. “The government did not shy away from its concern about partisanship in decisions made in the Presidential Records Act.”

“Today's argument really, really underscored the stakes of the litigation,” she said.

Sarah Weicksel, who leads the American Historical Association, stressed the importance of safeguarding an accurate account of the most powerful political office on the globe.

“It's not just a question about this moment,” she said. “This is a question about what is preserved, and what we will be able to learn about ourselves and what future Americans will be able to learn about us in 10, 20, 50, 100 years.”

entries.title: D.C. Police Start Enforcement Campaign Targeting E-Scooters and Bikes
entries.summary: The safety push comes a week after a senior D.C. official was killed in a scooter crash.
entries.content:
D.C. is cracking down on unsafe electric scooter and bike riders amid an uptick in traffic fatalities across the city.

The Metropolitan Police Department kicked off a street-safety outreach program Friday to address “unsafe behaviors” on micromobility vehicles, one week after a fatal e-scooter crash killed a D.C. man who worked in city government. The city has seen a 62% increase in deadly traffic accidents this year compared to the same period in 2025, according to District data.

“One of the areas where we’ve seen increased injuries and fatalities are e-scooters and e-bicycles,” said Interim Police Chief Jeffery Carroll during a brief gaggle with reporters at the corner of Seventh and H Streets NW, where e-scooters and bikes were zipping by. “E-bikes and e-scooters go much faster than regular foot-powered scooters and bicycles, so the nature of the injuries that can occur is much more intense.”

The outreach program is a District-wide initiative but will focus on areas with high concentrations of e-scooters and e-bikes, including Navy Yard, Chinatown and the U-Street corridor, MPD said Friday.

Outreach will continue through the end of the year, with officers handing out flyers warning riders to wear helmets, obey the rules of the road, avoid riding on the sidewalk in the Central Business District, and avoid using headphones while moving. Police will also remind people not to ride with more than one person on e-bikes and e-scooters.

There have been six fatalities this year involving the vehicles: four on e-bikes and two on e-scooters, MPD told The Washington Sun. Two other collisions, one involving an e-bike and one an e-scooter, resulted in "major crash response," but the victims were not killed. MPD did not provide data for the total number of collisions involving e-bikes and scooters this year.

The new enforcement campaign comes amid broader concerns about the growing popularity of e-scooters and e-bikes in D.C. and beyond. While proponents say they offer people easy ways to get around, many jurisdictions have struggled with kids and teenagers driving recklessly on e-bikes and scooters that in some cases can travel up to 46 miles an hour.

D.C. has made recent efforts to crack down on kids and teenagers using e-scooters and e-bikes from shared rental companies like Lime and Veo, and last year the companies took the step of limiting speeds on the vehicles in areas where teens gathered.

The District averaged 45,000 daily rides on e-bikes and e-scooters in 2026 as of Sept. 30, according to the District Department of Transportation Ride Report database.

The most recent fatality occurred Oct. 9 on Capitol Hill, when two scooters crashed at the intersection of Eighth St. and Pennsylvania Ave. SE. One of the riders — later identified as Talib Shakir, the director of the Mayor’s Office of Returning Citizens Affairs — died at the scene. Neither rider was wearing a helmet, Carroll said, and police believe one of the scooters was traveling at high speed.

District law does not require adults to wear a helmet, but it’s strongly encouraged. People must be 18 to rent and ride e-bikes and scooters.

A 2022 study from the University of California, San Francisco, found that riders who didn’t wear a helmet were almost twice as likely to sustain a head injury if involved in an e-bike crash as those who did wear helmets.

Katie Van Dyck, a D.C. resident who said she witnessed the crash that killed Shakir, wrote on social media Friday that there should be more rules around the use of e-scooters and e-bikes.

“We need stronger helmet laws and stricter rules for e-scooter and e-bike operation. Bike share and scooter companies have a real responsibility to better police who uses their products. Free helmet programs should be more frequent and easier to access. Residents shouldn't have to walk into a police station to get one. And we need more bike lanes that actually connect,” she wrote.

Some residents have called on the D.C. Council to impose more restrictions on e-scooters and e-bikes, including mandating that they be registered and that users have insurance. Carroll didn’t share specifics, but he told The Sun that new regulations are being considered.

“We are working with the mayor’s office and DDOT on regulations around these,” he said. “We are looking at that, if there are updates that need to be made.”

entries.title: Judge Threatens to Sanction Trump Over Skipped Deposition in $10 Billion BBC Suit
entries.summary: Judge Enjoliqué A. Lett said the president has repeatedly disregarded court procedures in an already costly legal fight for the British broadcaster.
entries.content:
A federal judge has threatened to sanction President Donald Trump for backing out of a deposition today in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué A. Lett said the president has repeatedly flouted court-ordered “meet and confer” obligations to participate in the discovery phase of the lawsuit.

“The Court has admonished [Trump] for his lack of participation to no avail,” Lett wrote in a Friday order. “Going forward, the Court expects strict compliance with its order, the failure of which will lead to sanctions.”

Trump was scheduled to sit for a deposition Friday as he seeks financial compensation from the BBC, whose journalists spliced together two different parts of a speech he gave on Jan. 6, 2021, before the Capitol insurrection. Late last month, his lawyers canceled the session, citing "matters of national importance" and proposed pushing Trump’s testimony to January 2027.

The president is in Georgia to campaign for Senate candidate Mike Collins and gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson on Friday, and he’s scheduled to travel to Mar-a-Lago later in the evening.

The suit has proven costly for the BBC, with analysts estimating that defense costs could reach $100 million. The news broadcaster has already been forced to file five separate appeals due to Trump’s “disregard” of the court’s discovery procedures, Lett wrote.

entries.title: Voting Rights Groups Are Backing California Over DOJ’s Noncitizen Voting Lawsuit
entries.summary: The groups say the Trump administration’s lawsuit over 20,000 potential noncitizens who received a mail-in ballot defies “basic standards of decency.”
entries.content:
Voting rights groups want to quickly step into the Justice Department’s lawsuit against California as the Trump administration seeks to block the state from counting the votes of over 20,000 people it says could be noncitizen voters.

The League of United Latin American Citizens and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, in a filing Friday, said the DOJ’s actions “flout the law, disregard the realities of election administration, and defy basic standards of decency — all while voting is underway.”

The DOJ gave California a letter and a password-protected thumb drive, along with the password attached on a sticky note, with a list of voters it believed were potential noncitizens who received a mail-in ballot through California’s universal vote-by-mail system.

The state was given 48 hours to comply with checking whether each citizen was a voter, which would have meant checking 417 names per hour. Now, the DOJ is suing California for not complying with that letter.

LULAC and the NAACP argue that they can intervene as organizations that represent vulnerable groups to protect civil and political rights. They also argue that their interference is not premature because of the looming deadline of Election Day.

“The Federal Government seeks to control which voters may remain on California’s voter rolls, which ballots get counted, and which steps voters must take to prove their citizenship,” the filing says. “Such drastic alterations to California election procedures — sought at the eleventh hour — would have immense effects on [the voting groups’] election-related work and their members’ ability to vote.”

The administration is not backing down from pursuing California’s voters. Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, told Fox News on Friday that the government would be seeking an emergency order forcing California to set those 20,000 ballots aside.

The groups’ request could be denied by the court, though Friday’s request also mentions that the case has yet to get a judge or set a date.

“They are only interested in protecting California voters’ and their members’ ability to engage in meaningful political participation, including casting a ballot and having that ballot counted alongside the ballots of other eligible California voters,” the groups’ filing says.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Legal Groups Are Suing to Stop ‘Fast-Tracking’ of Child Asylum Claims
entries.summary: Trump administration policies give short notice for interviews of children who arrived in the U.S. without a parent.
entries.content:
A group of legal service providers for immigrant families filed a lawsuit Thursday in an effort to halt Trump administration policies they say are unlawfully rushing the deportation of children seeking asylum after arriving in the U.S. without a parent.

The providers say U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Executive Office for Immigration Review have recently started giving short notice of asylum interviews to unaccompanied children and their attorneys and blocking attorneys from rescheduling interviews, even when they’ve been double-booked.

“Their attorneys are expected to represent children in multiple asylum interviews on the same day, sometimes at the same time, forcing them to forgo preparation and severely limiting their ability to effectively represent their unaccompanied child clients,” the lawsuit says. “For these children, who risk being sent back to the countries they fled, the stakes could not be higher.“

It’s worse for detained unaccompanied children, who are told they must immediately file asylum applications and are given only 24 hours before an interview, the lawsuit says. Immigration judges have been ordered to complete all those cases by Jan. 31.

The six groups bringing the federal lawsuit in Maryland are Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, The Door, the Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, Immigrant Defenders Law Center, and Jewish Family and Community Services Pittsburgh.

Lawyers for the groups said USCIS’s and EOIR’s policies break from decades of bipartisan legislation in which Congress declared migrant children who arrive in the U.S. unaccompanied as “uniquely vulnerable,” and therefore entitled to the right to a non-adversarial interview and representation by “qualified, independent attorneys.”

Now, they say the agencies are expediting a process that would normally take weeks to a matter of days. The groups say they’ve collectively received more than 600 notices of asylum interviews since August 1.

The complaint noted examples of children being required to continue asylum interviews even though they are visibly distressed and of attorneys frantically coordinating simultaneous interviews after their requests to reschedule have been ignored or denied.

“The United States guarantees unaccompanied children an immigration system that meets their unique needs. EOIR’s and USCIS’s new policies make those guarantees a hollow promise,” the lawsuit says. “This is not the immigration process that Congress intended for unaccompanied children; it is a deportation assembly line depriving them of their rights.”

The Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

entries.title: Zelenskyy Calls Starlink Restrictions ‘Very Painful’ as Trump Denies Responsibility
entries.summary: The Ukrainian president says the network’s reduced speeds have yet to be fully restored.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump is denying he had any part in the recent restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink network that prevented Ukraine from intercepting Russian drone attacks this week.

When asked by reporters who had prior knowledge of the disruptions, which Ukrainian authorities say were linked to at least five civilian deaths, Trump said “it wasn’t me, and it wasn’t Elon.”

“I didn’t do that,” he told reporters Friday. “No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning.”

The disruption occurred as Trump was pressuring Kyiv to stop striking Russian refineries, representing a further deterioration of the already contentious relationship between Trump and Zelenskyy. Ukrainian officials have asserted the Trump administration and SpaceX’s Elon Musk intentionally slowed satellite internet speeds to force Zelenskyy into accepting Trump's energy ceasefire.

Minutes after his statements Friday, The Telegraph reported that Musk had approached Trump directly with the plan to throttle Ukraine’s Starshield satellite internet network. But after Russia launched a series of deadly attacks on Kyiv following the new restrictions, Musk deflected.

“He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the U.S. administration that did it,” a senior source told the Telegraph. “The reality is that they were both in it.”

Musk said Wednesday that Washington controls Starshield, and that the U.S. military and Trump are the ones to determine implementing restrictions.

Zelenskyy said transmission speeds had yet to be fully restored to their previous rates but confirmed the effort was underway.

His statements Friday echoed the bipartisan outrage among U.S. lawmakers, including two Republicans on the Senate Intelligence Committee who signed a bipartisan letter calling on Pentagon Inspector General Platte Moring to launch an investigation.

“We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered ‘shaheds’ that attack our civilians and kill families,” the Ukrainian leader wrote on X. “We couldn’t use a tool that helps protect people. That’s very painful and frustrating.”

Zelenskyy said Ukraine uses the network to intercept Russia’s Shahed drones, strike targets in occupied Ukrainian territory and deliver food and water to troops by drone — not to carry out attacks over the Russian border.
